title: Windows on the Nothing Phone (3a) - Part 4: Booting Windows
tags: UEFI, Windows, Qualcomm, Mu-Silicium, ARM64, Reverse Engineering, ACPI
content: Where we are After Part 3 the phone boots Mu-Silicium to the logo with storage, buttons, USB and mass storage working. This part is about Windows: Making room on the phone’s storage (an ESP and a Windows partition). Building a Windows PE that drops to a command prompt, and putting it on the ESP. A crash caused by the memory map. A long silent hang, and the method I used to find it without a debugger. The cause: a GUID. Making Windows see the phone’s storage. Installing full Windows. The order is the order things happened. Sections 3 to 5 are where most of the day went, and I think they are the most useful part of this series, because the technique works for any “it just hangs” problem on any device. Making room: partitioning What Windows needs An ESP: FAT32, GPT type EF00. Holds Boot Manager, the BCD, and (for WinPE) the boot image. I made it 2 GiB because WinPE’s boot.wim is 700+ MB. A Windows partition: NTFS, GPT type 0700 (Microsoft basic data). Everything else. On a phone, the only big partition is userdata. So: shrink userdata, put the new partitions after it. Android keeps working, with less space. This wipes Android’s data. userdata is encrypted per-device, and resizing it means Android has to format it on next boot. Back up anything you care about. And keep the GPT backup from Part 2. Looking at the table adb root adb shell sgdisk --print /dev/block/sda On my phone the main LUN (sda) uses 4096-byte sectors (UFS usually does), so sector numbers are 4 KiB units, not the 512-byte units you may be used to. userdata was partition 13, the last one, running to the end of the disk (234 GiB). The new layout I wanted 64 GiB for Android. 64 GiB / 4 KiB = 16,777,216 sectors. userdata started at sector 2,449,992, so: # Name Start End Size Type 13 userdata 2449992 19227647 64 GiB Android data (unchanged type GUID and unique GUID) 14 esp 19227648 19751935 2 GiB EF00 15 win 19751936 61390842 158.8 GiB 0700 I copied this approach from my OnePlus phone, where I had done the same thing earlier with sgdisk from a root shell. On the phone: sgdisk --delete=13 \ --new=13:2449992:19227647 \ --typecode=13:1B81E7E6-F50D-419B-A739-2AEEF8DA3335 \ --partition-guid=13:4B7839CC-3B42-5B66-9F3C-08919267C764 \ --change-name=13:userdata \ --new=14:19227648:19751935 --typecode=14:EF00 --change-name=14:esp \ --new=15:19751936:61390842 --typecode=15:0700 --change-name=15:win \ /dev/block/sda sgdisk --verify /dev/block/sda Notes: Recreating userdata with its original type GUID and unique partition GUID matters. Android finds it by name, but some firmware and init scripts check the GUIDs too. Read both with sgdisk --info=13 /dev/block/sda before deleting. The kernel will not see the new partition bounds while userdata is mounted, so reboot. The old userdata contents do not survive the resize; I did a factory reset, and after it df -h /data showed 64 GiB and Android booted normally. Use /dev/block/by-name/esp and /dev/block/by-name/win from now on, never /dev/block/sda14. On one boot, the main LUN showed up as sdc instead of sda. Formatting from the phone My phone’s root shell has newfs_msdos and mkfs.ntfs, so no PC is needed: newfs_msdos -F 32 -S 4096 -c 1 -L ESP /dev/block/by-name/esp mkfs.ntfs -f -s 4096 -L Windows /dev/block/by-name/win -S 4096 tells the FAT formatter the real sector size. Get this wrong and UEFI’s FAT driver may refuse the filesystem. The 32-entry GPT problem sgdisk --print also told me the GPT on sda only has room for 32 partition entries. The UEFI spec requires at least 128, and recent Windows versions are known to “fix” non-compliant GPTs on their own, which on a phone can be disastrous. A dry run (sgdisk --resize-table=128 on a copy of the table) showed the larger table fits without moving any partition. I have not applied it yet; it has to happen before a full Windows boot touches the disk. If you do this yourself, do it at the same time as repartitioning. Getting a Windows image Which Windows Windows on ARM builds come as .esd files. I used Windows 11 25H2, build 26200, ARM64, the consumer “multi-edition” ESD. Mu-Silicium’s status page says recent Qualcomm generations need Windows builds 26090 or newer; older builds do not support the newest CPU cores. wimlib-imagex info 26200.9550...A64FRE_EN-US.esd lists the images in it. Mine had six; index 1 is Windows 11 Pro. Building a WinPE from the install image Microsoft’s “real” WinPE comes with the Windows ADK, which only runs on Windows. But every install image already contains a WinPE: the recovery environment. mkdir -p ~/woa/winpe && cd ~/woa/winpe wimlib-imagex extract ~/Downloads/26200*.esd 1 \ /Windows/System32/Recovery/winre.wim --dest-dir=. --no-acls (The path is case-sensitive inside the ESD: winre.wim, lowercase. My first try with Winre.wim silently extracted nothing.) WinRE starts a recovery UI via winpeshl.ini. Delete that file and it runs startnet.cmd, which leaves you at a command prompt: cp winre.wim boot.wim wimlib-imagex update boot.wim 1 --command="delete /Windows/System32/winpeshl.ini" The boot files come from the install image too: wimlib-imagex extract ~/Downloads/26200*.esd 1 \ /Windows/Boot/DVD/EFI/BCD /Windows/Boot/DVD/EFI/boot.sdi \ /Windows/Boot/EFI/bootmgfw.efi /Windows/Boot/EFI/en-US /Windows/Boot/Fonts \ --dest-dir=boot --no-acls Boot/DVD/EFI/BCD is the BCD Windows uses on its install DVD: one entry, “Windows Setup”, that RAM-boots \sources\boot.wim using \boot\boot.sdi. That is exactly what we need. The ESP layout: EFI/Boot/bootaa64.efi (copy of bootmgfw.efi, the fallback path) EFI/Microsoft/Boot/bootmgfw.efi EFI/Microsoft/Boot/BCD EFI/Microsoft/Boot/Fonts/... EFI/Microsoft/Boot/en-US/... boot/boot.sdi sources/boot.wim Reading and editing the BCD on Linux The DVD BCD has boot debugging enabled for the boot manager (element 26000010, bootdebug). With bootdebug on, Boot Manager tries to talk to a debugger on a serial port that does not exist. I wanted that off. A BCD is a registry hive. You can read it with the Python library regipy: from regipy.registry import RegistryHive h = RegistryHive('BCD') for k in h.recurse_subkeys(as_json=False): print(k.path) Each boot object is a key under \Objects\{GUID}, each setting a key under Elements\<hex id> with an Element value. 26000010 is a boolean stored as one byte. Changing one byte in an existing value does not change the hive’s structure, so I wrote a tiny script that finds that element’s data cell and flips it from 01 to 00, then verified with regipy that it reads back as 0. (On Windows, bcdedit /store BCD /set {bootmgr} bootdebug off does the same.) Writing the ESP from Android With mass storage blocked on my laptop (Part 3), I wrote the ESP from Android. This took some trial and error: adb shell sessions each get their own mount namespace. A mount made in one adb shell is invisible in the next one, and adb push cannot write into it. So everything (mount, copy, sync, unmount) must happen in one shell session. I first streamed a tar through adb exec-in. It silently truncated boot.wim by 1.8 MB. Always verify with sha256sum. The reliable way: push to /data/local/tmp, then in one session mount the ESP, copy, sync, checksum, unmount: #!/bin/bash # esp_sync.sh <local ESP tree>: replace the phone's ESP contents, verified by sha256 set -e T=$(realpath "$1") adb root >/dev/null adb shell 'rm -rf /data/local/tmp/espstage && mkdir -p /data/local/tmp/espstage' for d in "$T"/*; do adb push "$d" /data/local/tmp/espstage/ >/dev/null; done (cd "$T" && find . -type f -print0 | sort -z | xargs -0 sha256sum) > /tmp/esp.local adb shell ' for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do mkdir -p /mnt/esp_t mount -t vfat /dev/block/by-name/esp /mnt/esp_t 2>/dev/null && break; sleep 2; done rm -rf /mnt/esp_t/EFI /mnt/esp_t/boot /mnt/esp_t/sources cp -r /data/local/tmp/espstage/. /mnt/esp_t/ && sync cd /mnt/esp_t && find . -type f ! -name "*.txt" | sort | while read f; do sha256sum "$f"; done cd /; umount /mnt/esp_t; rmdir /mnt/esp_t; rm -rf /data/local/tmp/espstage' > /tmp/esp.remote diff <(sort -k2 /tmp/esp.local) <(sort -k2 /tmp/esp.remote) && echo "ESP synced and verified" The retry loop on mount is there because the previous session’s mount sometimes lingers for a second (“Device or resource busy”). Right after Android boots, adb root also needs a few seconds before the shell is really root. Crash 1: the memory map First boot with WinPE on the ESP. Mu-Silicium found Boot Manager, loaded it, and crashed almost immediately: Synchronous Exception ... External abort FAR 0x0000000080000000 in BdsDxe (the boot manager part of our firmware), not in Windows. Symbolizing the crash address against Build/.../BdsDxe.dll with llvm-symbolizer --relative-address pointed to the Kernel Errata Patcher (Part 1). KEP watches Boot Manager allocate memory, and at one point it reads memory that Boot Manager had just allocated as LoaderCode. That memory was at 0x80000000. Remember Part 1: on this phone, DRAM starts at 0x80000000, and the first chunk of it belongs to the Gunyah hypervisor. Reading it from EL1 is an external abort: the hypervisor refuses the access. But why did the firmware give that memory to Boot Manager? Our memory map from xbl_config did not list anything at 0x80000000. And Mu-Silicium’s RamManagerDxe reads the total RAM layout from Qualcomm’s shared memory and adds every range not in our map as free RAM. So the gap became free memory. Finding every hole The source of truth for “which memory may the OS use” is the device tree Android booted with. Two nodes: /memory: the RAM ranges the kernel is allowed to use at all, /reserved-memory: carve-outs inside those, with no-map meaning “do not even map this”. I wrote two short scripts that walk the DTB structure directly (no libraries needed, the format is simple) and print both: # memnode.py: print /memory reg ranges from a DTB import struct, sys d = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read() off_struct, off_str = struct.unpack_from('>II', d, 8) def s(o): return d[off_str + o: d.index(b'\0', off_str + o)].decode() p = off_struct; path = [] while True: tok = struct.unpack_from('>I', d, p)[0]; p += 4 if tok == 1: # FDT_BEGIN_NODE e = d.index(b'\0', p); path.append(d[p:e].decode()); p = (e + 4) & ~3 elif tok == 3: # FDT_PROP ln, no = struct.unpack_from('>II', d, p); p += 8; v = d[p:p+ln]; p = (p + ln + 3) & ~3 if len(path) == 2 and path[1].startswith('memory') and s(no) == 'reg': for i in range(0, len(v), 16): b, l = struct.unpack_from('>QQ', v, i) print('%010x-%010x %10.1f MiB' % (b, b + l, l / 2**20)) elif tok == 2: path.pop() # FDT_END_NODE elif tok == 4: continue # FDT_NOP elif tok == 9: break # FDT_END $ python3 memnode.py Resources/DTBs/asteroids.dtb 0080e00000-0081800000 0081cf5000-0081cff000 0081f20000-00824a0000 0082800000-008ac00000 ... 0880000000-08afafe000 08b0000000-08b9700000 08bf800000-0900000000 0900000000-0a00000000 The first usable RAM starts at 0x80e00000, not 0x80000000. Everything between the listed ranges belongs to someone else. The rsvmem.py script (same walker, for /reserved-memory children) names the owners: gunyah_hyp, tme, chipinfo, smem, adsp_mhi, pvm_fw, hyp_mem_database, tz_stat, the modem/DSP firmware regions, wlan_msa, cpusys_vm, qtee, trusted_apps… Then compare every gap against my MemoryMapLib.c and add a reserved entry for each one not already covered: {"NOMAP", 0x80000000, 0x016E0000, AddMem, MEM_RES, UNCACHEABLE, Reserv, UNCACHED_UNBUFFERED_XN}, {"TME", 0x81CA0000, 0x00044000, AddMem, MEM_RES, UNCACHEABLE, Reserv, UNCACHED_UNBUFFERED_XN}, {"ChipInfo", 0x81CF4000, 0x0000C000, AddMem, MEM_RES, UNCACHEABLE, Reserv, UNCACHED_UNBUFFERED_XN}, {"ADSP_MHI", 0x81F00000, 0x00020000, AddMem, MEM_RES, UNCACHEABLE, Reserv, UNCACHED_UNBUFFERED_XN}, {"HYP_Reserved", 0x825A0000, 0x00260000, AddMem, MEM_RES, UNCACHEABLE, Reserv, UNCACHED_UNBUFFERED_XN}, {"WLAN_MSA", 0xA6400000, 0x00C00000, AddMem, MEM_RES, UNCACHEABLE, Reserv, UNCACHED_UNBUFFERED_XN}, {"CPUSYS_VM", 0xE0600000, 0x00400000, AddMem, MEM_RES, UNCACHEABLE, Reserv, UNCACHED_UNBUFFERED_XN}, {"QTEE_Tags", 0xE8900000, 0x00C00000, AddMem, MEM_RES, UNCACHEABLE, Reserv, UNCACHED_UNBUFFERED_XN}, {"HYP_Reserved_Hi0", 0x8AFAFE000,0x00502000, AddMem, MEM_RES, UNCACHEABLE, Reserv, UNCACHED_UNBUFFERED_XN}, {"HYP_Reserved_Hi1", 0x8B9700000,0x06100000, AddMem, MEM_RES, UNCACHEABLE, Reserv, UNCACHED_UNBUFFERED_XN}, Don’t forget memory above 4 GiB. Two hypervisor holes were up at 0x8AFAFE000 and 0x8B9700000; a map that only covers the low 4 GiB would hand those out too. The attributes copy what other Silicium devices use for no-map regions (MEM_RES, uncached, reserved). With those entries, the crash was gone. The FAT fix While I was at it, I applied a patch from topaz-woa (a Mu-Silicium port for the Redmi Note 12 4G that boots Windows) to the FAT driver in Mu_Basecore. Qualcomm phones have several small partitions with FAT-looking contents, some of which claim to be larger than their partition or are FAT12. The EDK2 FAT driver can hang on those. The patch rejects FAT volumes larger than their partition and skips FAT12. On my phone it fired on 8 partitions. It did not fix anything I could see, but it removed a suspect. The silent hang Now Boot Manager loaded, the screen kept showing the Silicium logo… and nothing else happened. No error, no crash dump, no Windows logo. I waited three minutes several times. The same thing happened with the RELEASE build. This is the worst kind of bug: no output. Here is how I approached it. Step 1: list the possibilities At this point, Boot Manager was running and had stopped making progress. Candidates: it is waiting for something (a timer, a device), it is extremely slow (storage reading at KB/s), it crashed, but its crash handler shows nothing, the hypervisor stalled it. Step 2: log firmware calls Boot Manager uses firmware services until ExitBootServices. So I made the firmware log every Boot Services call it received. In Mu-Silicium, KEP already hooks into the boot at the ReadyToBoot event, so I added a small diagnostic module there that replaces function pointers in the Boot Services table with wrappers that log and then call the original. The last calls before the hang: GetMemoryMap -> BUFFER_TOO_SMALL, then Success AllocatePages (Address, LoaderData, 2 pages) FreePages AllocatePages (Address, LoaderCode, 128 pages @ 0x82120000) -> Success <nothing> After that allocation, Boot Manager made no further firmware calls: no disk reads, no timer checks. And my own 2-second heartbeat timer stopped printing too. Step 3: write diagnostics to files instead of the screen Reading tiny log text off a phone screen via photos wasted a lot of time (I misread hex digits more than once and went down a wrong path because of it). So I changed the approach: the diagnostic module waits until the ESP is mounted (it hooks LoadImage, which runs right after the file system is up) and writes text files to the ESP root: memmap.txt: the full UEFI memory map at the moment Boot Manager starts bench.txt: a quick read benchmark of the ESP pmu.txt: the CPU performance counter configuration later, acpi.txt: every ACPI table the firmware installed On screen, it prints one line: [DIAG] ESP write memmap/bench/pmu/acpi.txt = Success After the test, back in Android, I mount the ESP and read them: adb shell 'mkdir -p /mnt/esp_t && mount -t vfat /dev/block/by-name/esp /mnt/esp_t && cat /mnt/esp_t/memmap.txt; umount /mnt/esp_t' Writing a file from UEFI is short: locate EFI_SIMPLE_FILE_SYSTEM_PROTOCOL on the ESP’s handle, OpenVolume, Open with create mode, Write, Close. PrintLib’s AsciiSPrint formats the text. What the files ruled out: Suspect Result Slow storage 4K reads 88 MB/s, 64K 627 MB/s, 1M ~1 GB/s. Fine Bad memory map 117 descriptors, every usable range inside DT /memory, every no-map region reserved The 0x82120000 allocation That is normal RAM (the RAMOOPS neighborhood), inside an allowed range Memory we can’t write Wrote and read back the first page of every free region: all 14 passed PMU / timer Cycle counter enabled, ~1.6 GHz; timer frequency 19.2 MHz as expected Boot debugger Off in the BCD Newer Boot Manager A completely different WinPE (an older 19041-based “driverless” one) hung the same way That last one was important: two Boot Manager versions years apart hung identically. So it was not a Boot Manager bug. It was something in our environment. Step 4: get symbols for Boot Manager To go further I needed to know where Boot Manager was, which meant reading it. Microsoft publishes symbols for it. Every PE file has a debug directory entry with a “RSDS” record holding the PDB name, a GUID and an age. Extract them: import struct, sys d = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read() i = d.find(b'RSDS') g = d[i+4:i+20]; age = struct.unpack_from('<I', d, i+20)[0] name = d[i+24:d.index(b'\0', i+24)].decode().split('\\')[-1] d1, d2, d3 = struct.unpack_from('<IHH', g) gid = '%08X%04X%04X%s%X' % (d1, d2, d3, g[8:].hex().upper(), age) print(f'https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols/{name}/{gid}/{name}') python3 pdburl.py bootmgfw.efi curl -L -A "Microsoft-Symbol-Server/10.0.0.0" -o bootmgfw.pdb \ "https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols/bootmgfw.pdb/C6B0B2AA4429A57378F7820C96619A772/bootmgfw.pdb" llvm-pdbutil dump -publics bootmgfw.pdb > publics.txt llvm-objdump -d --no-show-raw-insn bootmgfw.efi > bootmgfw.s publics.txt entries look like: 542340 | S_PUB32 [size = 32] `BlUtlGetAcpiTable` flags = function, addr = 0001:1865888 0001:1865888 means section 1 (.text), offset 1865888 decimal. .text starts at RVA 0x1000 in this binary, and the image base is 0x10000000, so: RVA = 0x1000 + 1865888 = 0x1000 + 0x1C78A0 = 0x1C88A0 VA = 0x10000000 + RVA = 0x101C88A0 I wrote a small script that loads all publics into a sorted list and annotates the disassembly with function names, so bootmgfw.s reads like BlInitializeLibrary+0x33c: bl MmArchInitialize. With that, I could read Boot Manager’s startup sequence. BlInitializeLibrary initializes, in order: firmware interface, boot debugger, devices, architecture (exception vectors, EL handling), memory manager (MmFwGetMemoryMap, then the page allocator, heap, …), time, logging, security, crypto, TPM, I/O, and so on. Then BmMain opens the BCD, picks an entry, loads the next stage. The 128-page LoaderCode allocation was inside the memory manager setup. After that, Boot Manager does a lot of work without calling the firmware at all, so “no more firmware calls” did not necessarily mean “stuck right there”. I needed a way to see how far it actually got. Step 5: breakpoints as checkpoints The idea from Part 1: replace one instruction with brk #0. If execution reaches it, the CPU takes an exception, the firmware’s handler prints a crash dump with ELR pointing at my breakpoint, and I know execution got there. If the logo just sits there, it did not. # bmbrk.py <in> <out> <VA>...: put brk #0 at virtual addresses in a PE file import struct, sys src, dst = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2] d = bytearray(open(src, 'rb').read()) pe = struct.unpack_from('<I', d, 0x3c)[0] ns = struct.unpack_from('<H', d, pe + 6)[0] so = pe + 24 + struct.unpack_from('<H', d, pe + 20)[0] base = struct.unpack_from('<Q', d, pe + 24 + 24)[0] secs = [struct.unpack_from('<8sIIII', d, so + 40 * i) for i in range(ns)] def off(va): # VA -> file offset, using the section table for name, vsize, vaddr, rsize, raw in secs: if base + vaddr <= va < base + vaddr + rsize: return raw + va - base - vaddr for spec in sys.argv[3:]: va = int(spec, 16); o = off(va) print('brk at', hex(va), 'was', hex(struct.unpack_from('<I', d, o)[0])) struct.pack_into('<I', d, o, 0xD4200000) # brk #0 open(dst, 'wb').write(d) My first breakpoint, at the start of MmArchInitialize: no dump, just the hang. A breakpoint even earlier, at a function I knew had run: also no dump. Breakpoints were not producing dumps at all. Why: Part 1 again. Whoever owns VBAR_EL1 owns crash handling. Boot Manager installs its own exception vectors very early (in ArchInitializeContext), so my brk went to Boot Manager’s handler, not the firmware’s. Boot Manager’s handler, with no debugger attached, just spins. The fix for testing: in my test copy of Boot Manager, replace the instruction that writes VBAR_EL1 with a nop, so the firmware’s handler stays in place. I found the writes by searching the disassembly: grep -n "msr.*VBAR_EL1" bootmgfw.s There were two: one in ArchInitializeContext (0x102a1d84) and a second in ArchSetExceptionState (0x102a1e78), which re-installs Boot Manager’s vectors every time it switches execution context. My first attempt only removed the first one, which is why my first “results” were wrong: the second write put Boot Manager’s handler back. With both removed, I ran a control test: a breakpoint at MmFwGetMemoryMap, which I knew ran because it called the firmware. It printed a dump. The method worked. Always run a control. A test that cannot fail tells you nothing. A breakpoint at a place you know is reached proves the method before you trust any “not reached” result. Boot Manager also checks its own image when it starts, so a modified copy needs that accounted for too. These patched copies were only ever test builds on my ESP; the final setup uses the original, unmodified Boot Manager. Walking forward Then it was a loop. Pick a point, plant a breakpoint, build, push to the ESP, boot, read the result: python3 bmbrk.py bootmgfw.vbar.efi bootmgfw.brkX.efi 0x101bbee8 cp bootmgfw.brkX.efi esp/EFI/Boot/bootaa64.efi cp bootmgfw.brkX.efi esp/EFI/Microsoft/Boot/bootmgfw.efi ./esp_sync.sh esp # boot, look for a dump, reboot to Android The firmware’s dump shows ELR, and the “Loading driver at” line for bootmgfw.efi gives the load base for that boot, so ELR minus base gives the RVA, which should match the breakpoint. Checkpoint Reached? MmFwGetMemoryMap yes MmArchInitialize entry yes after MmArchInitialize returns yes firmware init, logging, security, crypto yes TPM init (call and return) yes I/O init, TCB launch init, resource init yes end of BlInitializeLibrary yes BCD opened (BmpOpenStoreAndUpdateOptions) yes boot entry selected (BmpGetSelectedBootEntry) yes BlImgStartBootApplication (WinPE RAM disk and winload loaded) yes BlpArchTransferToEfiBootApplication (jump to winload) yes All of Boot Manager worked. The “no firmware calls after the 128-page allocation” was a red herring: it was just doing work that did not need the firmware. The hang was later. Into winload and the kernel Same technique, one level deeper. winload.efi lives inside boot.wim, so each test meant replacing it in the WIM: wimlib-imagex extract esp/sources/boot.wim 1 /Windows/System32/Boot/winload.efi --dest-dir=. --no-acls # ... patch it ... wimlib-imagex update esp/sources/boot.wim 1 \ --command="add winload.brk.efi /Windows/System32/Boot/winload.efi" wimlib-imagex update with several --command options in one call silently applied none of them for me. One command per call, then extract and sha256sum to verify the file really changed. winload’s symbols are winload_prod.pdb (same download method), image base 0x180000000. It also writes VBAR_EL1 in two places, which I noped in the test copy. The kernel’s PDB is ntkrnlmp.pdb, image base 0x140000000, with its own vector table setup in KiInitializeExceptionVectorTable. For the kernel tests, the test copy of winload also had its check of the kernel image relaxed, since the kernel was modified too. Checkpoint Reached? winload OslMain yes winload OslArm64TransferToKernel (after ExitBootServices) yes kernel entry KiSystemStartup yes KiInitializeKernel yes InitBootProcessor yes MmInitSystem call different result Two interesting things here. First, firmware crash dumps still printed after ExitBootServices, because the firmware’s vector table and framebuffer were still mapped. Second, the last test did not stop at my breakpoint. It produced a real crash. The real crash Data abort, translation fault, level 3 FAR = 0x0000000000000000 ELR = 0x00000000CE952AA0 A NULL pointer read. And the ELR was not in the kernel. That boot’s log said: Loading driver at 0x000CE78A000 EntryPoint=0x000CE7C8130 bootmgfw.efi So: 0xCE952AA0 - 0xCE78A000 = 0x1C8AA0 (RVA in bootmgfw.efi) From earlier, BlUtlGetAcpiTable starts at RVA 0x1C88A0. So the crash was at BlUtlGetAcpiTable+0x200, in Boot Manager’s code. (Parts of Boot Manager’s library stay in use while the next stages run, so an address in it showing up late is not strange.) The disassembly at that point: ; BlUtlGetAcpiTable+0x1f0 ... bl BlMmMapPhysicalAddressEx ; map an XSDT entry's physical address ... ldr w8, [x0] ; read the table's 4-byte signature <- crash, x0 = 0 BlUtlGetAcpiTable walks the XSDT, maps each entry, and compares its signature to the one it wants. One of the XSDT’s entries was zero. Lookups stop at the first match, so tables that came before the bad entry were found fine, and any lookup that had to walk past it crashed. That also explained why the behavior had seemed inconsistent. To keep these dumps readable on the phone screen, I trimmed Mu_Basecore’s exception handler output (no vector registers, no stack dump) to a compact summary with the faulting module and offset. Small change, big time saver. The cause: a GUID Time for the last diagnostic file. acpi.txt walks the RSDP and XSDT and prints every entry’s address, signature, length and OEM ID: RSDP CFE35018 rev 2 RSDT 0 XSDT CFE35F18 XSDT len 52 entries 2 [0] 0 NULL [1] CFE35B18 BGRT len 56 oem QCOM Two entries. One NULL, one BGRT (the boot logo table). No APIC, no FACP, no GTDT, no DSDT, no SSDT. None of my ACPI tables were installed at all. No interrupt controller description, no timers, no CPUs. Windows got remarkably far without them. Mu-Silicium’s ACPI platform driver installs tables from a firmware file found by GUID, PcdAcpiTableStorageFile, defined in MdeModulePkg.dec: 7E374E25-8E01-4FEE-87F2-390C23C606CD Every device’s AcpiTables.inf in Silicium-ACPI uses that as its FILE_GUID: $ grep -rh FILE_GUID Silicium-ACPI/Platforms/*/*/AcpiTables.inf | sort | uniq -c 50 FILE_GUID = 7E374E25-8E01-4FEE-87F2-390C23C606CD 1 FILE_GUID = 9FD3388E-2945-4017-B8D0-9781BDA5D80B That 1 was mine. In Part 2, when I created the file, I gave it a fresh random GUID, the same way I had for my library copy. The build was happy. UEFI was happy (it does not need ACPI). Android was happy (it does not use ACPI). The ACPI driver found no file with the expected GUID and installed nothing, and the only table in the XSDT was BGRT, which a different driver adds. The NULL entry was a side effect of an empty table list. One line: FILE_GUID = 7E374E25-8E01-4FEE-87F2-390C23C606CD Rebuilt, booted with the original, unmodified WinPE on the ESP… and a Windows command prompt appeared on the phone. Placeholder: add the photo of the WinPE prompt. If a firmware component “does nothing” with no error, check how it is found. A wrong GUID, name or path fails silently almost everywhere in UEFI. Was the breakpoint hunt wasted? No. Without it I would not have known that Boot Manager, winload and the kernel were all fine, and the NULL pointer in BlUtlGetAcpiTable was what pointed at ACPI. But had I compared my new files against existing devices at the start (that grep | uniq -c takes one second), I would have saved most of a day. Do that for every file you create from a template. Making Windows see the storage WinPE runs from RAM, so it booted without any storage driver. A full Windows installation needs to read its own partition. At the WinPE prompt: diskpart list disk would have nothing to show: the ACPI tables I copied from Palawan (DSDT_Minimal) only describe the CPUs. Windows does not know a UFS controller exists. Windows already has a UFS driver Windows ships a UFS storage driver, storufs.sys. Its INF lists the hardware it supports. I extracted it from the WinPE image to read it: wimlib-imagex extract winre.wim 1 /Windows/INF/storufs.inf --dest-dir=. --no-acls iconv -f utf-16 -t utf-8 storufs.inf | grep -iE "QCOM|^\[" [Qualcomm.NTarm64] %ACPI\QCOM24A5.DeviceDesc%=UfsQualcomm8996Install, ACPI\QCOM24A5 So any ACPI device with _HID QCOM24A5 gets the inbox driver. (The install section is named after the Snapdragon 820, “8996”, and is still used for newer Qualcomm UFS controllers.) Other Silicium devices’ DSDTs use the same ID. Writing the ACPI device The controller’s details come from the DT: python3 fdtq.py Resources/DTBs/asteroids.dtb ufshc /soc/ufshc@1d84000 compatible qcom,ufshc /soc/ufshc@1d84000 reg ['0x1d84000', '0x3000', '0x1d88000', '0x18000'] /soc/ufshc@1d84000 reg-names ufs_mem ice /soc/ufshc@1d84000 interrupts ['0x0', '0x109', '0x4'] /soc/ufshc@1d84000 dma-coherent [] (fdtq.py is the same FDT walker as memnode.py, printing properties of nodes whose name contains a string.) Registers at 0x1D84000. For the size I used 0x15000, the same value the Waipio and Nothing Phone (2) DSDTs use for their UFS0 at this address; it covers the UFS register block. Interrupt: SPI 0x109 → GSIV 0x109 + 32 = 0x129 (Part 1). dma-coherent → _CCA = 1. I checked the Snapdragon 8 Gen 1 (Waipio) DSDT in Silicium-ACPI: its UFS0 device has the same address and interrupt, which was reassuring. I created Silicium-ACPI/Silicon/Qualcomm/Milos/DSDT_Minimal.asl: Palawan’s minimal DSDT (eight CPU devices) plus: Device (UFS0) { Name (_HID, "QCOM24A5") Name (_UID, 0) Name (_CCA, 1) Name (_CRS, ResourceTemplate () { Memory32Fixed (ReadWrite, 0x01D84000, 0x00015000) Interrupt (ResourceConsumer, Level, ActiveHigh, Exclusive, ,, ) { 0x129 } }) Method (_STA, 0, NotSerialized) { Return (0x0F) } Device (DEV0) { Name (_ADR, 8) Name (_RMV, 0) } } DEV0 is the storage device on the controller, marked not removable (Windows treats removable disks differently, and will not install onto them). Compiling it I did not have iasl installed, and no sudo on this machine. Project Mu publishes it as a NuGet package (edk2-acpica-iasl), which is just a zip: mkdir -p ~/woa/iasl && cd ~/woa/iasl curl -sSL -o p.nupkg "https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/projectmu/acpica/_packaging/mu_iasl/nuget/v3/flat2/edk2-acpica-iasl/20230628.0.1/edk2-acpica-iasl.20230628.0.1.nupkg" unzip -oq p.nupkg chmod +x edk2-acpica-iasl/Linux-x86/iasl cd Silicium-ACPI/Silicon/Qualcomm/Milos ~/woa/iasl/edk2-acpica-iasl/Linux-x86/iasl DSDT_Minimal.asl # Compilation successful. 0 Errors, 0 Warnings Point the device’s INF at it: [Binaries] ASL|Common/SSDT.aml ASL|Palawan/APIC.aml ASL|Milos/DSDT_Minimal.aml ASL|Palawan/FACP.aml ASL|Palawan/GTDT.aml Rebuilt, booted WinPE, diskpart, list disk: a 234 GB disk. That is UFS LUN 0, the one with userdata, esp and win. Windows could see the phone’s storage with its own inbox driver, with no Qualcomm driver package at all. As far as I can tell this works because the controller is already initialized and the device started when Mu-Silicium hands over (that START UNIT patch from Part 3 again). Installing Windows The usual way to install Windows on these phones is: boot UEFI in mass storage mode, plug into a Windows PC, and run dism and bcdboot there. I had no Windows PC and a laptop that blocks USB disks. So I built the Windows partition on Linux and wrote it to the phone with fastboot. Applying the image on Linux wimlib can apply a Windows image directly onto an NTFS filesystem using the NTFS-3G library. In that mode it keeps everything Windows needs: security descriptors (ACLs), reparse points, hard links, short names. (Applying to a mounted directory does not, and the result will not boot.) The win partition is sectors 19751936 to 61390842, so 41,638,907 sectors of 4096 bytes. Create a sparse file of exactly that size, format it, apply: mkdir -p ~/woa/install && cd ~/woa/install truncate -s $((41638907 * 4096)) win.raw mkntfs -F -Q -s 4096 -p 19751936 -L Windows win.raw wimlib-imagex apply ~/Downloads/26200*.esd 1 win.raw -F: it is a file, not a device; -Q: quick format. -s 4096: the disk’s sector size. -p 19751936: the partition’s start sector, stored in the NTFS boot sector. mkntfs warns “Windows will not be able to boot from this device” because the CHS geometry fields are empty; that only matters for BIOS booting from the partition itself, not for UEFI. The file is 158.8 GiB on paper but only takes the space of the data written to it (about 18 GB), because it is sparse. Applying index 1 extracted 16 GiB of files, 215,766 of them. Converting to a fastboot sparse image fastboot flash can write “Android sparse” images, which only carry the non-empty blocks. Convert: img2simg win.raw win.simg 4096 (The block size is a positional argument. img2simg -b 4096 is not a thing, I tried.) The result is about 18 GB. Flashing adb reboot bootloader fastboot getvar partition-size:win fastboot flash win win.simg fastboot splits the image into chunks the bootloader can accept (max-download-size was 768 MB on my phone) and writes them one by one. 18 GB over USB takes a while. Watch the output; it prints each chunk. fastboot flash only writes the one partition you name. It does not touch userdata, boot or anything else. Still, double check the partition name before pressing enter. Boot files The installed Windows needs its own Boot Manager and BCD on the ESP, pointing at the win partition. That is what bcdboot does, and WinPE has it. Boot Mu-Silicium with WinPE still on the ESP, and at the prompt: diskpart list vol exit Find the letter of the 158 GB NTFS volume labeled “Windows” (say C:), then: bcdboot C:\Windows /f UEFI bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled no bcdedit /set {default} bootstatuspolicy IgnoreAllFailures bcdedit /set {default} testsigning on bcdboot copies Boot Manager to the ESP and writes a new BCD with an entry for C:\Windows. It finds the ESP by its EF00 type. recoveryenabled no and bootstatuspolicy IgnoreAllFailures: if a boot fails, do not jump into automatic repair. On a device like this, automatic repair cannot fix anything and only hides the real error. testsigning on: needed later, for community drivers (touch, USB host) that are not signed by Microsoft. This replaces the WinPE boot files on the ESP. I keep the WinPE tree on my PC, so putting it back is one esp_sync.sh away. Where things stand As I write this:     Mu-Silicium UEFI boots, display, storage, buttons, USB, mass storage Windows PE boots to a command prompt Internal storage in Windows visible through the inbox UFS driver Full Windows image built and being written to the win partition; bcdboot and first boot to setup are next What is left, roughly in order: Finish the install and boot to Windows setup (OOBE). Without touch or a keyboard, I will not get far into it, but reaching it proves the full boot path. Resize the GPT to 128 entries before Windows touches the disk for real. USB host mode in ACPI (an XHCI controller device, like topaz-woa does), so a USB keyboard and mouse work through a USB-C hub. Proper ACPI tables for Milos: right now APIC, FACP and GTDT are Palawan’s, and only CPUs and UFS are described. Clean up: the diagnostic module and the compact exception handler come out, the FAT fix goes in properly, and the memory map and ACPI fixes are committed (the GUID fix and the memory map reservations already are). I will update this post when Windows reaches setup. Lessons from this part Copy-and-modify is how ports start, and also where they go wrong. Diff every new file against two or three existing devices. My one-day bug was a single line that a grep | uniq -c would have caught. The memory map is a security boundary. On a hypervisor-based phone, memory you do not own faults. Compare your map against DT /memory and /reserved-memory, including above 4 GiB. Silence is information. “No firmware calls after X” and “no crash dump” both meant something different from what they first suggested. Prove your observation method with a control before trusting a negative result. Get diagnostics off the screen. Text files on the ESP, read from Android, were faster and more accurate than photos of a log. Symbols are free. Microsoft’s symbol server turns Windows binaries from a wall of hex into named functions. BlUtlGetAcpiTable+0x200 told me more than an hour of guessing. Bisect everything. Drivers, boot stages, kernel init: pick a midpoint, test, halve. Credits This would have taken much longer without the work of others: Project Silicium for Mu-Silicium, Silicium-ACPI and the WoA-Guides. The patch authors credited in Binaries/asteroids/README.md: Gustave Monce, Robotix, Kancy Joe, Shandorman and N1kroks. topaz-woa for the FAT and memory map work and USB host notes. woa-pong (Nothing Phone (2)), the Renegade Project, Port-Windows-11-Xiaomi-Pad-5, mu_aloha_platforms and edk2-gunyah for references along the way. Microsoft, for Project Mu and for public symbols.

title: Windows on the Nothing Phone (3a) - Part 3: Going Green
tags: UEFI, Qualcomm, Mu-Silicium, ARM64, Reverse Engineering
content: Where we are At the end of Part 2 the firmware started, printed its log, loaded twenty-odd drivers, and stopped at: Loading driver at 0x000... PmicDxe.efi This part goes from there to a fully booted UEFI: the Silicium logo, working storage, buttons, USB, and mass storage. In Status.md terms: Feature State at the end of this part Display working Internal Storage working Side Buttons working USB Device Mode working Mass Storage working USB Host Mode not tested yet USB Power Delivery not tested yet Windows Boot / Linux Boot Part 4 Most of this part is about one skill: reading and patching closed-source ARM64 binaries. Qualcomm does not give us source for its drivers. When one hangs, we disassemble it, figure out what it is waiting for, and change a few bytes so it stops waiting. Tools for this part # disassemble a whole driver /usr/lib/llvm-18/bin/llvm-objdump -d --no-show-raw-insn PmicDxeLa.efi > pmic.s # disassemble a few bytes at a file offset xxd -s 0x13120 -l 24 -p PmicDxeLa.efi | sed 's/../0x& /g' | \ /usr/lib/llvm-18/bin/llvm-mc --disassemble -triple=aarch64 -mattr=+v9.2a # assemble one instruction to get its bytes echo 'mov w0, wzr' | /usr/lib/llvm-18/bin/llvm-mc -triple=aarch64 -show-encoding # compare two binaries byte by byte (offsets are decimal, values octal) cmp -l Original.efi Patched.efi I wrapped the second command in a tiny Python helper because I used it hundreds of times: # aadis.py: disassemble n instructions at a file offset import subprocess def dis(path, off, n=6): d = open(path, 'rb').read()[off:off + 4*n] src = ' '.join('0x%02x' % b for b in d) r = subprocess.run(['/usr/lib/llvm-18/bin/llvm-mc', '--disassemble', '-triple=aarch64', '-mattr=+v9.2a,+mte,+pauth'], input=src, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout lines = [l.strip() for l in r.splitlines() if l.strip() and not l.strip().startswith('.')] for i, l in enumerate(lines): print(' %06x %s' % (off + 4*i, l)) One thing to know when reading llvm-mc output: it prints branch targets as offsets relative to the instruction, not absolute addresses. bl #24668 at 0x13128 means a call to 0x13128 + 24668 = 0x13128 + 0x605C = 0x19184. llvm-objdump on the whole file prints absolute addresses instead, which is easier to follow when you are reading a full function. For Qualcomm’s small DXE drivers, the code section’s file offset and its virtual address are the same, so the offsets in this post are both file offsets and RVAs. Check this for your own binaries (Part 1 explains the conversion); for large Microsoft binaries it is not true. Porting other people’s patches Before writing any patches of my own, I ported the ones that already exist for bale_b, the donor device. Every device folder in Binaries has a README.md describing its patches, and keeps both the stock file and the .patched.efi one. bale_b’s list: Driver Patch Why SPMIDxe Stub out the SPMI handle function Crash during boot PmicDxe Make a failing SPMI write call return success Hang during boot ClockDxe Remove the Clock_CESTADisableDependencies call Keep some clocks on TzDxeLA Flip a global “TZ applet” flag from FALSE to TRUE Crash during boot UFSDxe Replace the sleep call with a wakeup, plus a hibernate-exit Use internal storage ButtonsDxe Map the power button to ENTER instead of SUSPEND Usable power button UsbConfigDxe Do not de-initialize USB at ExitBootServices USB keeps working in the OS UsbMsdDxe Report the disk as non-removable Mass storage behaves The patches are tied to bale_b’s binaries. My binaries are built from the same boot branch, so the code is mostly the same, but at different offsets, with different addresses in branch instructions. Copying bytes at the same offsets would corrupt random code. The process for each patch: Step 1: see exactly what the donor changed cd Binaries/bale_b/QcomPkg/Drivers/ClockDxe cmp -l ClockDxe.efi ClockDxe.patched.efi cmp -l prints every differing byte (offset in decimal, then old and new values in octal). Convert the first offset to hex, then disassemble both files there: bale_b ClockDxe.efi @ 0xa514: sub sp, sp, #64 stp x29, x30, [sp, #16] ... bale_b ClockDxe.patched.efi @ 0xa514: mov w0, #0 ret So the patch replaces the start of a function with “return 0”. Now I need the same function in my ClockDxe. Step 2: find the same code in your binary Searching for the exact bytes fails. Most instructions are identical between the two builds, but anything that encodes an address relative to itself (bl, b, adrp, cbz, ldr literal) changes when code moves. So I search with those parts masked out. For each instruction, keep the opcode bits and register fields, zero the immediate offset, and compare: # fuzzy.py: find code from one binary in another, ignoring PC-relative offsets import struct def mask(w): if (w & 0x7C000000) == 0x14000000: return w & 0xFC000000 # b / bl if (w & 0xFF000010) == 0x54000000: return w & 0xFF00001F # b.cond if (w & 0x7E000000) == 0x34000000: return w & 0xFF00001F # cbz / cbnz if (w & 0x7E000000) == 0x36000000: return w & 0xFFF8001F # tbz / tbnz if (w & 0x1F000000) == 0x10000000: return w & 0x9F00001F # adr / adrp if (w & 0x3B000000) == 0x18000000: return w & 0xFF00001F # ldr literal if (w & 0x7F800000) == 0x11000000: return w & 0xFFC003FF # add imm (page offsets) if (w & 0x3B000000) == 0x39000000: return w & 0xFFC003FF # ldr/str unsigned offset return w def words(path): d = open(path, 'rb').read() return [struct.unpack_from('<I', d, i)[0] for i in range(0, len(d) - 3, 4)] def find(src, soff, dst, before=8, after=8): s = words(src); t = words(dst); i0 = soff // 4 pat = [(k - i0, mask(s[k])) for k in range(i0 - before, i0 + after) if 0 <= k < len(s)] return [j * 4 for j in range(len(t)) if all(0 <= j + r < len(t) and mask(t[j + r]) == m for r, m in pat)] >>> find('bale_b/.../ClockDxe.efi', 0xa514, 'asteroids/.../ClockDxe.efi') [0xa66c] Exactly one match means the same code is at 0xa66c in my binary. Zero matches means the code changed (shrink the window with before/after, or read both functions by hand). Two or more means the pattern is too short. The masks come from the ARM instruction encoding tables. You do not need all of them memorized; the ones above cover the instructions that commonly differ between builds. Step 3: verify by reading, then patch Always disassemble your match and the donor’s original side by side and read them. Same instructions, same structure, same registers? Then apply the patch at your offset: import struct d = bytearray(open('ClockDxe.efi', 'rb').read()) assert struct.unpack_from('<I', d, 0xa66c)[0] == 0xD10103FF # sub sp, sp, #64 (sanity check) struct.pack_into('<I', d, 0xa66c, 0x52800000) # mov w0, #0 struct.pack_into('<I', d, 0xa670, 0xD65F03C0) # ret open('ClockDxe.patched.efi', 'wb').write(d) The assert is important. If you run the script on the wrong file, or twice, it stops instead of silently corrupting something. Then point the INF at the patched file: [Binaries.AARCH64] DXE_DEPEX|ClockDxe.depex|* PE32|ClockDxe.patched.efi|* Keep the stock file next to it. You will want to compare against it later. Where each bale_b patch landed on my phone Driver bale_b offset My offset Change SPMIDxe   0x154c, 0x2e58 mov w0, #0; ret PmicDxe   0x1c6ac mov w0, #0; ret (SPMI write wrapper) ClockDxe 0xa514 0xa66c mov w0, #0; ret TzDxeLA   byte 0xe5a8 0 → 1 UFSDxe   0xa528 see the UFS section below ButtonsDxe   0x3cc0 mov w8, #13; b #-76 UsbConfigDxe 0x565c 0x561c cbz → b UsbMsdDxe 0x3ff0 0x3ff0 mov w8, #0x80 → mov w8, #0 UsbMsdDxe happened to be at the same offset in both builds. Most were not. The TzDxe flag TzDxe’s patch is not code, it is data: one byte in the data section that holds a global boolean. To port it, I found which instructions read that byte in bale_b’s binary (its cross references), found the same instructions in mine with the fuzzy matcher, and followed their adrp + ldrb to the address they read. In my binary it was file offset 0xe5a8, read from code at 0x2fc0 and 0x3320: d = bytearray(open('TzDxeLA.efi', 'rb').read()) assert d[0xe5a8] == 0 d[0xe5a8] = 1 open('TzDxeLA.patched.efi', 'wb').write(d) The buttons patch A good example of a patch that changes behavior rather than skipping something. In ButtonsDxe, the power button’s key code is loaded into w8 and then the code jumps to the common “report key” path: stock: patched: 3cb8 cmp w15, #1 3cb8 cmp w15, #1 3cbc b.ne #12 3cbc b.ne #12 3cc0 mov w8, #258 (0x102) 3cc0 mov w8, #13 (ENTER) 3cc4 b #-168 3cc4 b #-76 0x102 is the UEFI scan code for SUSPEND, which does nothing useful in a menu. The patch loads 13 (carriage return, ENTER) instead, and jumps to the path that reports a character key rather than a scan code. So the power button selects menu items. UsbConfigDxe stock: patched: 5618 ldrb w8, [x8, #2233] 5618 ldrb w8, [x8, #2233] 561c cbz w8, #52 561c b #52 In the ExitBootServices handler, a flag decides whether to tear down the USB controller. Turning the conditional cbz into an unconditional b always takes the “skip teardown” path. Hang 1: PmicDxe With all bale_b patches ported, the log still stopped at PmicDxe. The PMIC (Power Management IC) is the chip that supplies every voltage rail on the board, handles the power key, charging and the battery. Qualcomm phones have several PMIC chips, and the SoC talks to them over a two-wire bus called SPMI. PmicDxe initializes them through SPMIDxe. bale_b’s patches make SPMI calls return success instead of crashing (our firmware is not allowed to do some PMIC writes the way Qualcomm’s own UEFI did). That fixes a crash, but creates a new problem: any code that writes a PMIC register and then waits for it to change will now wait forever, because the write never actually happened. Patches from other devices Other ports on the same boot branch (muyu, peridot, salami) had one more PmicDxe patch: “Removed PMIC Post Init”. I found the matching code in my binary with the fuzzy matcher: two bl calls inside PmicDxe’s main init sequence: 3910 mov w19, w0 3914 bl #64340 <- post-init step 3918 orr w19, w0, w19 391c bl #58056 <- post-init step Replacing both with mov w0, wzr makes them “return success” without running. Rebuilt, tested: still stuck at PmicDxe, with no new log lines. Bisecting a binary No new lines means I had no idea where inside PmicDxe it was stuck. The driver’s entry function runs a long list of init steps. So I built six test images, each making PmicDxe return success at a different point: Image How much of PmicDxe runs cut0 nothing, return immediately at the entry point cut1 setup only, before the main init function cut2 the first 3 init steps cut3 2 more steps cut4 1 more step cut5 almost everything The patch for a “cut” is simple: at the cut point, set the status register to 0 and jump to the function’s epilogue (its cleanup and ret): # cut.py <in> <out> <variant> import struct, sys src, dst, variant = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], int(sys.argv[3]) d = bytearray(open(src, 'rb').read()) put = lambda off, w: struct.pack_into('<I', d, off, w) b = lambda pc, t: 0x14000000 | (((t - pc) >> 2) & 0x3FFFFFF) # encode "b target" MOV_X0_XZR, RET, MOV_W21_WZR = 0xAA1F03E0, 0xD65F03C0, 0x2A1F03F5 if variant == 0: put(0x1148, MOV_X0_XZR); put(0x114C, RET) # entry point elif variant == 1: put(0x15CC, MOV_X0_XZR); put(0x15D0, RET) # main init else: cut = {2: 0x15F4, 3: 0x1618, 4: 0x1684, 5: 0x1698}[variant] put(cut, MOV_W21_WZR) # the function keeps its status in w21 put(cut + 4, b(cut + 4, 0x16D8)) # jump to the epilogue at 0x16d8 open(dst, 'wb').write(d) How I picked these addresses: I read the main init function in the full disassembly (llvm-objdump), found its epilogue (the block that restores registers and returns, at 0x16d8), noticed it returns w21 as its status, and picked cut points between the bl calls of the init sequence. Then I built one image per variant and booted them in order. The result: cut0 to cut4: the log went past PmicDxe (later drivers loaded, some complained, which is expected when PMIC setup is skipped) cut5: stuck at PmicDxe So the hang was in the steps between cut4 and cut5: two calls, to 0x1514 and 0x1305c. Finding the loop 0x1305c was the battery init function. Inside it: 13120 tst w8, w10 13124 b.eq #28 13128 bl #24668 -> 0x19184 1312c mov w19, w0 13130 bl #31780 -> 0x1ad54 13134 orr w19, w0, w19 Reading 0x19184 and 0x1ad54: both are battery and charger detection routines. They write PMIC registers to start a detection, then poll a status register in a loop until it reports done. With PMIC writes disabled, the detection never starts, and the poll never ends. The fix (I called it fixA) replaces just those two calls: 13128 mov w0, wzr 1312c mov w19, w0 13130 mov w0, wzr 13134 orr w19, w0, w19 import struct d = bytearray(open('PmicDxeLa.patched.efi', 'rb').read()) bl = lambda pc, t: 0x94000000 | (((t - pc) >> 2) & 0x3FFFFFF) for pc, t in ((0x13128, 0x19184), (0x13130, 0x1AD54)): assert struct.unpack_from('<I', d, pc)[0] == bl(pc, t) # really the call we expect struct.pack_into('<I', d, pc, 0x2A1F03E0) # mov w0, wzr open('PmicDxeLa.patched.efi', 'wb').write(d) I also built a fixB that skipped the whole battery init function, as a fallback. I did not need it. fixA got past PmicDxe. Patch the narrowest thing that works. Skipping a whole init function may “fix” the hang and break something unrelated later, and you will not know which patch caused it. A side note: PmicDxe’s own logs PmicDxe has its own debug prints, filtered by a print mask stored in the binary (at file offset 0x2946c, value 0x80000400) and a second filter (b.eq at 0x493c). Patching those makes it print much more. I used that once while chasing this hang; it showed nothing useful because the hang was before any print, which is why the bisect was needed. Still worth knowing. Hang 2: UFSDxe Past PmicDxe, the log now stopped at UFSDxe with: ufs_error_log: 11 ufs_error_log: 96 ufs_error_log: fffffffb What UFS needs at boot UFS storage has two parts: the host controller inside the SoC (at 0x1D84000 on this chip) and the UFS device (the flash chip). They talk over a high-speed serial link. The controller is commanded with UIC commands (link-level: power modes, hibernate) and SCSI commands (data-level: read, write, start unit). When the phone’s bootloader hands over, the link and the device can be in different states: link active or in hibernate (a low power link state), device powered on or stopped. The UEFI driver must bring both to active before reading anything. Decoding the error log ufs_error_log prints numbers, not messages, so I searched the disassembly for where each value is passed to the logging function. 0x11 is logged when a UIC command completes but reports failure. 0x96 identifies the call site: the command being sent was 0x18, DME_HIBERNATE_EXIT, “wake the link from hibernate”. fffffffb is -5, EFI_DEVICE_ERROR. That command was not in the stock driver’s path. It came from the patch I ported from bale_b, which had two parts: Replace a call that puts the device to sleep with a call that sends SCSI START STOP UNIT with “active”. A code cave (extra code written into unused space in the binary) that sends DME_HIBERNATE_EXIT first, because on bale_b the bootloader leaves the link in hibernate. On my phone the link was already active. Exiting hibernate when you are not in hibernate fails. And bale_b’s cave, on failure, logs the error and jumps back to its own start, so it retries forever. That is the hang. Three test images Image Contents Result ufsA both parts, but the cave continues on failure instead of looping long register dump, then ASSERT ... Device Error, reboot. The failed hibernate exit left the link broken ufsB stock UFSDxe, no patch short trace, ASSERT, reboot. But the trace showed the device answering: SCSI sense data 70 00 02 ... 04 02 ufsC stock UFSDxe + part 1 only works ufsB was the useful failure. SCSI sense data is how a storage device explains why it refused a command: 70: standard sense format sense key 02: NOT READY additional sense code 04, qualifier 02: “logical unit not ready, initializing command required” In plain terms: “I am fine, but someone needs to send me a START UNIT command.” That is exactly what part 1 of bale_b’s patch does. So ufsC kept only part 1: stock: ufsC: a520 cmp w20, #208 a520 cmp w20, #208 a524 b.ne #116 a524 b.ne #116 a528 bl #5724 -> 0xbb84 a528 mov x1, #1 a52c cbnz w0, #-80 a52c bl #6020 -> 0xbcb0 a530 mov x0, x19 a530 mov x0, x19 0xbb84 is the stock call (it checks the state and fails when the device is stopped). 0xbcb0 is the function that sends START STOP UNIT; x1 = 1 is the “start, active” argument. With ufsC, the log went past UFSDxe, past the rest of the drivers, and the screen showed the Silicium logo. UEFI booted. Ported patches encode assumptions about the donor’s bootloader. Read what each part does, and test the parts separately. “Patch from a similar phone” is a starting point, not a fix. Boot messages that look scary but are fine With UEFI booting, the DEBUG log had a few errors: IQSEEComCompatAppLoader_loadFromBuffer failed ret = 16 (featenabler app) SPSS not supported ... Pwload - ERR - fail! The first is TrustZone refusing to load the featenabler secure app. It only affects FeatureEnablerDxe, which nothing we need depends on. SPSS (the secure processor subsystem) is not used in UEFI on this chip and is skipped. Pwload comes from GpiDxe failing to load firmware for GPI, a DMA engine used by I2C/SPI controllers. They still work without it, just slower. None of them block anything. The way to judge an error message: find which driver prints it, and ask whether anything you need depends on that driver. Buttons With the ButtonsDxe patch, volume up/down move through the menu and power selects. Nothing else to do. Side buttons: green. Display The display was “working” since the very first boot, because we never drive the display hardware. ABL already turned the panel on and set up a framebuffer at 0xE3940000 to show its splash. Mu-Silicium’s SimpleFbDxe just draws into that same buffer, at the resolution set in the dsc (1080 x 2392, 32 bits per pixel). Two things had to be right for that: the Display_Reserved entry in the memory map at the splash address, so nothing else allocates that memory, the SMMU detach in PlatformSecLib (Part 2), so the display engine reads physical memory directly. Windows also uses this framebuffer through the generic “Basic Display” driver, so no display driver is needed to see Windows. USB and mass storage Mu-Silicium’s front page has a Mass Storage option. It exposes UFS LUN 0 (the big one with userdata) to a PC as a USB disk. On the phone side, it worked once UsbConfigDxe and UsbMsdDxe were patched. On my laptop, it did not show up. This took a while, and none of it was the phone’s fault. What I checked on the PC lsusb # is the device there at all? dmesg -w # what does the kernel do when it attaches? journalctl -f | grep -iE "usb|scsi" The phone enumerated as 05c6:f000 in mass storage mode (it shows up as 045e:066b “Windows Flashing Capable Device” in plain UEFI USB mode). Then three separate things got in the way: usb_modeswitch. It has rules for 05c6:f000 because some 4G modems use that ID, and it tried to “switch” the phone into modem mode. Fix: DisableSwitching=1 in /etc/usb_modeswitch.conf. gvfs MTP. GNOME’s MTP volume monitor guessed it was a OnePlus phone in MTP mode and grabbed it. Fix: systemctl --user stop gvfs-mtp-volume-monitor.service. Endpoint security software. My work laptop runs Kaspersky’s endpoint agent with device control, which removes USB storage devices about 36 ms after they attach. That one I could not turn off. Proving the phone side works anyway Since the laptop would not let a USB disk exist, I talked to the phone’s mass storage directly with pyusb, sending SCSI commands myself the way the kernel’s usb-storage driver would. USB mass storage (“Bulk-Only Transport”) is simple: you send a 31-byte Command Block Wrapper containing a SCSI command, optionally read data, then read a 13-byte Command Status Wrapper. # msdprobe.py: talk SCSI to a USB mass storage device without the kernel driver import struct, usb.core, usb.util dev = usb.core.find(idVendor=0x05c6, idProduct=0xf000) if dev.is_kernel_driver_active(0): dev.detach_kernel_driver(0) usb.util.claim_interface(dev, 0) tag = 1 def cmd(lun, cdb, inlen): global tag # CBW: signature 'USBC', tag, data length, direction, LUN, CDB length, CDB cbw = struct.pack('<IIIBBB', 0x43425355, tag, inlen, 0x80 if inlen else 0, lun, len(cdb)) + cdb.ljust(16, b'\0') tag += 1 dev.write(0x01, cbw, timeout=3000) data = bytes(dev.read(0x81, inlen, timeout=3000)) if inlen else b'' csw = bytes(dev.read(0x81, 13, timeout=3000)) # CSW: 'USBS', tag, residue, status return csw[12], data st, d = cmd(0, bytes([0x12, 0, 0, 0, 36, 0]), 36) # INQUIRY print('INQUIRY', st, d[8:36]) st, d = cmd(0, bytes([0x00] * 6), 0) # TEST UNIT READY print('TEST UNIT READY', st) st, d = cmd(0, bytes([0x25] + [0] * 9), 8) # READ CAPACITY(10) last, bs = struct.unpack('>II', d) print('blocks', last + 1, 'block size', bs, 'GiB %.1f' % ((last + 1) * bs / 2**30)) usb.util.release_interface(dev, 0) dev.attach_kernel_driver(0) The result: INQUIRY answered, TEST UNIT READY passed, READ CAPACITY reported 234.2 GiB with 4096-byte blocks. That is LUN 0, exactly right. Once I had stopped usb_modeswitch and gvfs, the laptop did briefly see it as a disk with all thirteen partitions, before device control removed it again. So mass storage works. If you are on a normal Linux or Windows PC, it should just show up. If it does not, check for anything on the PC side that claims USB devices before blaming the firmware. This is also why I did the Windows install in Part 4 without mass storage. Most guides tell you to put the phone in mass storage mode and run dism from a Windows PC. I had neither a Windows PC nor a laptop that would allow it, so everything was done from Android and from Linux tools. Writing it down Two pieces of documentation for this part. Binaries/asteroids/README.md lists every patch: the driver, the reason, what changed, and who originally made it. Patch authors on Silicium are credited by name, and if you reuse their work you should do the same. Mine credits Gustave Monce (buttons), Robotix (clocks, PMIC), Kancy Joe (SPMI, PMIC, UFS), Shandorman (PMIC) and N1kroks (TzDxe, UFS), and notes which parts I changed for this phone (the extra PMIC battery-detection patch, and UFS without the hibernate exit). Status.md gets a section for the device: ## Nothing Phone (3a) **State:** Active <br> **Codename:** asteroids | Feature | Description | State | |:-------------------|:------------|:-----:| | Display | | ✅ | | Internal Storage | | ✅ | | Side Buttons | | ✅ | | USB Host Mode | | ❔ | | USB Device Mode | | ✅ | | USB Power Delivery | | ❔ | | Mass Storage | | ✅ | | Windows Boot | | ❔ | | Linux Boot | | ❔ | Then commit. In the Binaries submodule I committed one patch per commit, then the README, so anyone can see exactly which bytes each fix changed. Then the submodule pointer and Status.md in the main repo. What I learned in this part A hang in a closed driver is almost always a loop waiting for hardware. Bisect to find the function, then read it to find the loop. Build several test images at once. Each boot test costs a minute or two, and having cut0 to cut5 ready meant one sitting instead of six round trips. Port patches by meaning, not by offset. Masked pattern search finds the code; reading it confirms it. Every ported patch is someone else’s fix for someone else’s bootloader. When one does not work, split it into parts and test them separately. Use assert in every patch script. In Part 4 we make room for Windows on the phone, boot Windows PE, and spend a long time finding out why Windows Boot Manager hangs.

title: Windows on the Nothing Phone (3a) - Part 2: Setting Up the UEFI Project
tags: UEFI, Qualcomm, Mu-Silicium, ARM64, Reverse Engineering
content: Where we are In Part 1 I covered the theory: boot chains, ARM64, UEFI, ACPI, and how Windows boots. This part is practical. By the end of it we will have: a working build environment for Mu-Silicium, a full backup of the phone’s firmware, Qualcomm’s UEFI drivers extracted from the phone, the memory map and configuration pulled out of the stock firmware, a new SoC package (MilosPkg) and device package (asteroidsPkg), an image that ABL accepts and starts. It will not work yet. The first boot hangs halfway through the driver list. Fixing that is Part 3. I will show every command I ran. Paths like ~/woa/backup are just where I kept things; use whatever you like. Setting up the PC I used Ubuntu. Install the basics: sudo apt install git python3 python3-venv python3-pip clang lld llvm \ adb fastboot xxd binutils device-tree-compiler \ wimtools ntfs-3g android-sdk-libsparse-utils What each is for: clang, lld, llvm: the compiler Mu-Silicium uses, plus llvm-objdump (disassembler), llvm-mc (assembles single instructions) and llvm-pdbutil (reads Microsoft symbol files). On my machine they live in /usr/lib/llvm-18/bin/. adb, fastboot: talking to the phone. xxd: hex dumps. device-tree-compiler (dtc): decompiles device trees. If your distro does not have it, the Python fdt package does the same job, and that is what I ended up using. wimtools, ntfs-3g, android-sdk-libsparse-utils: only needed in Part 4, for Windows images. Getting Mu-Silicium git clone https://github.com/Project-Silicium/Mu-Silicium.git --recursive cd Mu-Silicium ./setup_env.sh -p apt python3 -m pip install -r pip-requirements.txt The clone is about 5 GB because of the submodules (Mu_Basecore, Binaries, Silicium-ACPI, OpenSSL and others). Before touching anything, build an existing device to prove the environment works: python3 build_uefi.py -d bale_b -r DEBUG If that ends with a Mu-bale_b.img in the repo root, your setup is fine. If it fails now, it is an environment problem, not a porting problem, and it is much easier to fix before you have added your own files. build_uefi.py options worth knowing: Option Meaning -d <device> Which device to build -r DEBUG / -r RELEASE DEBUG prints a log on the screen. Always use DEBUG while porting -c Clean build Python tools for poking at firmware I kept these in a virtual environment so they do not mess with the system Python: python3 -m venv ~/woa/venv ~/woa/venv/bin/pip install uefi_firmware fdt uefi_firmware gives you uefi-firmware-parser, which unpacks UEFI firmware volumes. fdt parses device tree blobs (.dtb) and can print them as source (.dts). Getting to know the phone Root shell My phone runs a userdebug ROM, so: adb root adb shell id # uid=0(root) On a retail ROM with Magisk you would run commands as adb shell su -c '...'. Everything below needs root. Identity adb shell getprop ro.product.device # asteroids adb shell getprop ro.product.model # A059 adb shell getprop ro.board.platform # volcano adb shell getprop ro.soc.model # SM7635 adb shell getprop ro.boot.slot_suffix # _b adb shell getprop ro.build.fingerprint adb shell cat /sys/devices/soc0/soc_id # 636 volcano is the name Android uses for this platform. Qualcomm’s bootloader uses yet another name, which we find in a moment. The partitions adb shell ls -l /dev/block/by-name/ You get a long list of links like uefi_b -> /dev/block/sde22. The ones I cared about are listed in Part 1. Note the active slot (_b for me). Everything we extract comes from that slot. Backing up the firmware Before anything else, dump every firmware partition. You will not flash any of these, but you will read them over and over, and if something ever does go wrong you want the originals. mkdir -p ~/woa/backup && cd ~/woa/backup for p in uefi_a uefi_b xbl_a xbl_b xbl_config_a xbl_config_b abl_a abl_b \ boot_a boot_b init_boot_a init_boot_b vendor_boot_a vendor_boot_b \ dtbo_a dtbo_b vbmeta_a vbmeta_b imagefv_a imagefv_b devcfg_a devcfg_b \ toolsfv uefisecapp_a uefisecapp_b; do adb exec-out "cat /dev/block/by-name/$p" > $p.img || echo "FAIL $p" done sha256sum *.img > SHA256SUMS adb exec-out streams raw bytes without the terminal mangling them (plain adb shell can convert line endings on some versions). Also save the partition table of the big LUN. We will change it in Part 4: adb exec-out 'sgdisk --backup=/tmp/sda.gpt /dev/block/sda >/dev/null 2>&1; cat /tmp/sda.gpt' > sda-gpt-sgdisk.bak adb shell sgdisk --print /dev/block/sda > sda-gpt.txt Finding the SoC’s UEFI name Mu-Silicium organizes Qualcomm SoCs by the name Qualcomm’s UEFI uses, not the marketing name. SM8635 (Snapdragon 8s Gen 3) is Palawan, SM8550 is Kailua, and so on. You find the name in the strings of the stock UEFI: strings uefi_b.img | grep -m3 -iE "Build/[A-Za-z]+" strings -n 8 uefi_b.img xbl_b.img | grep -m6 -oE "BOOT\.[A-Z0-9._-]+" On my phone: the build path contains Build/MilosLAA → the SoC is Milos, the boot chain version is BOOT.MXF.2.1-01955-LANAI-1.88923.2. That second string matters more than it looks. BOOT.MXF.2.1 is the branch of Qualcomm’s boot code. Phones on the same branch have very similar UEFI drivers, which means the binary patches other people made for their phone have a good chance of applying to yours with only the offsets changed. Choosing donors Milos was not in Mu-Silicium. So I needed two donors: An SoC package to copy. Palawan (SM8635) is the closest supported SoC: same generation, same GIC layout, same kind of CPU cores. So PalawanPkg → MilosPkg. A device package to copy. I looked for a supported device on the same boot branch, BOOT.MXF.2.1. The Realme GT Neo6 (bale_b, a Palawan phone) is on it, and its driver patches are documented. So bale_bPkg → asteroidsPkg. I also used patches from muyu, peridot and salami (other devices on the same branch) later, in Part 3. To check a device’s branch, look at the README.md in its Binaries/<device> folder. Most list the firmware version they were extracted from. Unpacking Qualcomm’s UEFI mkdir -p ~/woa/uefi_b && cd ~/woa/uefi_b ~/woa/venv/bin/uefi-firmware-parser -b -e -o . ~/woa/backup/uefi_b.img -b brute-forces the search for firmware volumes (Qualcomm wraps them in an ELF), -e extracts everything, -o . writes here. You get a tree like: volume-4096/ file-9e21fd93-.../section0/section1/volume-1d301fe9-.../ file-d93ce3d8-a7eb-4730-8c8e-cc466a9ecc3c/ section0.pe <- the driver section1.depex <- dependencies section2.ui <- name, in UTF-16 file-.../ ... Every file-<GUID> folder is one FFS file. To see what is what, print the names: for u in $(find . -name "*.ui"); do echo "$(tr -d '\0' < $u) $(dirname $u)" done | sort (.ui files are UTF-16, so stripping the zero bytes is a lazy way to turn them into ASCII.) You will see names like ClockDxe, PmicDxe, UFSDxe, UsbConfigDxe, ButtonsDxe, TzDxeLA, and also raw files like uefiplat.cfg, SecParti.cfg, uefipil.cfg, QcomChargerCfg.cfg, panel configs and logos. uefiplat.cfg Qualcomm’s UEFI reads platform settings from uefiplat.cfg. Print it: for u in $(find . -name "*.ui"); do [ "$(tr -d '\0' < $u)" = "uefiplat.cfg" ] && cat $(dirname $u)/section1.raw | tr -d '\r' done It has a [ConfigParameters] section with entries like: EnableShell = 0x1 SharedIMEMBaseAddr = 0x14680000 NumCpus = 8 NumActiveCores = 8 EnableUfsIOC = 1 UfsSmmuConfigForOtherBootDev = 1 ... Qualcomm’s drivers ask for these values at runtime through a configuration protocol. In Mu-Silicium, each device provides them in ConfigurationMapLib.c. For my phone, the values turned out to be identical to bale_b’s, which is another sign of how close devices on the same branch are. The memory map: the most important file in the port Where Qualcomm keeps it Qualcomm’s UEFI also needs a memory map, and older SoCs kept it in uefiplat.cfg as plain text. On newer ones it moved. I searched for region names I knew should exist: grep -boa "UEFI_FD\|DXE_Heap\|Sched_Heap" ~/woa/backup/*.img The hit was in xbl_config_b.img. Looking at the bytes around it with xxd showed device tree structure: property names, reg, and so on. xbl_config contains embedded device trees, and the memory map is one of them. Carving device trees out of a blob Every flattened device tree starts with the magic number d0 0d fe ed, followed by its total size (big-endian, 4 bytes). So finding them is a simple scan: # carve_fdt.py: extract every device tree blob from a binary file import struct, sys data = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read() out = sys.argv[2] i = 0; n = 0 while True: i = data.find(b'\xd0\x0d\xfe\xed', i) if i < 0: break size = struct.unpack('>I', data[i+4:i+8])[0] if 0x40 < size < len(data) - i: # ignore false matches open(f'{out}/fdt_{n}_{i:x}.dtb', 'wb').write(data[i:i+size]) print(hex(i), hex(size)); n += 1 i += 4 mkdir -p ~/woa/xblcfg python3 carve_fdt.py ~/woa/backup/xbl_config_b.img ~/woa/xblcfg # then decompile each one for f in ~/woa/xblcfg/*.dtb; do ~/woa/venv/bin/python -c "import fdt,sys; print(fdt.parse_dtb(open(sys.argv[1],'rb').read()).to_dts())" $f > ${f%.dtb}.dts done grep -n "uefimem" ~/woa/xblcfg/*.dts The second blob has a node with compatible = "qcom,uefimem", called memorymap. Each child is one region: memory@A7000000 { device_type = "memory"; reg = <0x0 0xA7000000 0x0 0x400000>; MemLabel = "UEFI_FD"; ResourceAttribute = <0x703C07>; BuildHob = [00]; ResourceType = [00]; MemoryType = [04]; CacheAttributes = [02]; }; That is exactly the information Mu-Silicium’s MemoryMapLib wants, just encoded as numbers. Decoding the numbers Mu-Silicium’s memory map entries look like this: // Name, Address, Length, HobOption, ResourceType, ResourceAttribute, MemoryType, ArmAttribute {"UEFI_FD", 0xA7100000, 0x00300000, AddMem, SYS_MEM, SYS_MEM_CAP, BsData, WRITE_BACK}, Each field corresponds to one DT property: DT property Values Mu-Silicium name BuildHob 0, 1, 4 AddMem, AddDev, NoHob ResourceType 0, 1, 5 SYS_MEM (RAM), MMAP_IO (registers), MEM_RES (reserved) ResourceAttribute 0x703C07, 0x400, 0x7 SYS_MEM_CAP, UNCACHEABLE, INITIALIZED MemoryType 0, 4, 6, 7, 0xB Reserv, BsData, RtData, Conv, MmIO CacheAttributes 0x02, 0x22, 0x23, 0x25, 0x00 WRITE_BACK, WRITE_BACK_XN, WRITE_THROUGH_XN, UNCACHED_UNBUFFERED_XN, NS_DEVICE I worked these out by comparing a device that already had both a DT memory map and a Mu-Silicium MemoryMapLib.c, and by reading MemoryMapLib.h and ArmLib.h in the source. XN means “execute never”: the CPU may not run code from that region. Instead of converting a hundred lines by hand, I wrote a script: # memmap.py: convert Qualcomm's qcom,uefimem DT node to MemoryMapLib entries import sys, fdt t = fdt.parse_dtb(open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read()) path = [n for n in t.walk() if n[0].endswith('memorymap')][0][0] node = t.get_node(path) HOB = {0:'AddMem', 1:'AddDev', 4:'NoHob'} RT = {0:'SYS_MEM', 1:'MMAP_IO', 5:'MEM_RES'} RA = {0x703C07:'SYS_MEM_CAP', 0x400:'UNCACHEABLE', 0x7:'INITIALIZED'} MT = {0:'Reserv', 4:'BsData', 6:'RtData', 7:'Conv', 0xB:'MmIO'} CA = {0x02:'WRITE_BACK', 0x22:'WRITE_BACK_XN', 0x23:'WRITE_THROUGH_XN', 0x25:'UNCACHED_UNBUFFERED_XN', 0x00:'NS_DEVICE'} def val(n, k): p = n.get_property(k) v = p.data if hasattr(p, 'data') else p.value return v[0] if isinstance(v, (list, bytes, bytearray)) else v for n in node.nodes: r = n.get_property('reg').data base = (r[0] << 32) | r[1]; size = (r[2] << 32) | r[3] name = n.get_property('MemLabel').value print(' {%-22s 0x%08X, 0x%08X, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s},' % ( '"%s",' % name, base, size, HOB[val(n,'BuildHob')], RT[val(n,'ResourceType')], RA[val(n,'ResourceAttribute')], MT[val(n,'MemoryType')], CA[val(n,'CacheAttributes')])) ~/woa/venv/bin/python memmap.py ~/woa/xblcfg/fdt_1_39e4c.dtb The output pastes almost directly into MemoryMapLib.c. Two adjustments, both copied from how bale_b does it: Qualcomm’s map has UEFI_FD at 0xA7000000, 4 MiB. Mu-Silicium splits it: FD_Reserved at 0xA7000000 (1 MiB) and UEFI_FD at 0xA7100000 (3 MiB). Our firmware image is loaded at 0xA7100000. Regions that only matter to Qualcomm’s own UEFI core (which we do not run) can be dropped. If unsure, compare with the donor device’s file. The part I got wrong at first The uefimem node only lists regions Qualcomm’s UEFI cares about. It does not list every piece of memory that belongs to the hypervisor, TrustZone, or other processors. And Mu-Silicium has a driver (RamManagerDxe) that takes the full RAM size from shared memory and fills every gap in your map with free RAM. So any carve-out missing from your map becomes “free memory” that Windows will happily allocate. My first Windows boot crashed reading 0x80000000, which belongs to the Gunyah hypervisor, for exactly this reason. The fix (in Part 4) was to compare the map against the Android device tree’s /memory and /reserved-memory nodes and add reserved entries for every hole. If you are doing this yourself, do that comparison now. I will show the method in Part 4. The device tree for the boot image ABL refuses to boot a kernel without a device tree it likes, matching the phone’s qcom,msm-id and qcom,board-id. The easiest DTB that ABL definitely accepts is the one it booted Android with: adb exec-out cat /sys/firmware/fdt > Resources/DTBs/asteroids.dtb xxd -l 16 Resources/DTBs/asteroids.dtb # starts with d00d feed strings Resources/DTBs/asteroids.dtb | grep -m3 -iE "volcano|asteroids|Nothing" /sys/firmware/fdt is the exact blob the kernel received. It is also a great reference for everything else: addresses of the UFS controller, the GIC, the SMMU stream IDs, the display’s reserved memory. You can read individual properties live: adb shell 'cd /sys/firmware/devicetree/base; cat model; echo; xxd -p qcom,msm-id; xxd -p qcom,board-id' adb shell 'cd /sys/firmware/devicetree/base/reserved-memory; xxd -p splash_region/reg' From it I got: What Value Where from GIC distributor 0x17100000 interrupt-controller@17100000 reg GIC redistributors 0x17180000 same node, second reg Splash framebuffer 0xE3940000, size 0x2B00000 reserved-memory/splash_region Display size 1080 x 2392 adb shell wm size CPU clusters 4 + 3 + 1 cpus/cpu-map MDP SMMU stream IDs 0x1C00, 0x1C01, 0x1C02 iommus of the display nodes Creating the SoC package: MilosPkg Start from Palawan: cd Silicon/Qualcomm mkdir MilosPkg cp -r PalawanPkg/Library MilosPkg/ Then write MilosPkg/MilosPkg.dsc.inc. This is included by every device on this SoC. The full file: [Defines] # # Timer # USE_PHYSICAL_TIMER = 0 # # KEP # HAS_ACTLR_EL1_UNIMPLEMENTED_ERRATA = 1 HAS_AMCNTENSET0_EL0_UNIMPLEMENTED_ERRATA = 1 HAS_GIC_V3_WITHOUT_IRM_FLAG_SUPPORT_ERRATA = 1 HAS_PSCI_MEMPROTECT_FAILING_ERRATA = 0 !include QcomPkg/QcomPkg.dsc.inc [BuildOptions] *_*_AARCH64_CC_FLAGS = -march=armv9.2-a+crypto+rcpc [PcdsFixedAtBuild] # # ACPI # gEfiMdeModulePkgTokenSpaceGuid.PcdAcpiDefaultOemTableId|0x202020534F4C494D gEfiMdeModulePkgTokenSpaceGuid.PcdAcpiDefaultOemRevision|0x7635 # # CPU # gArmPlatformTokenSpaceGuid.PcdCoreCount|8 gArmPlatformTokenSpaceGuid.PcdClusterCount|3 # # GIC # gArmTokenSpaceGuid.PcdGicDistributorBase|0x17100000 gArmTokenSpaceGuid.PcdGicRedistributorsBase|0x17180000 # # SMBIOS # gSiliciumPkgTokenSpaceGuid.PcdSmbiosProcessorModel|"Snapdragon (TM) 7s Gen 3 @ 2.50 GHz" gSiliciumPkgTokenSpaceGuid.PcdSmbiosProcessorPartNumber|"SM7635" [LibraryClasses] # # SEC Libraries # PlatformSecLib|MilosPkg/Library/PlatformSecLib/PlatformSecLib.inf [Components] # # Custom Drivers # QcomPkg/Drivers/IortDtDxe/IortDtDxe.inf Where each value came from: USE_PHYSICAL_TIMER = 0: under a hypervisor we use the virtual timer. Same as Palawan. KEP errata: copied from Palawan. Same CPU generation, same Windows quirks. Part 1 explains KEP. -march=armv9.2-a+crypto+rcpc: the CPU architecture level. Copied from Palawan. OEM table ID 0x202020534F4C494D: this is just the ASCII string "MILOS " read as a little-endian 64-bit number. It ends up in the header of every ACPI table. Compute it with: python3 -c "print(hex(int.from_bytes(b'MILOS ','little')))" OEM revision 0x7635: from the chip number SM7635. Other SoC packages follow the same pattern. Core and cluster count: from the DT cpu-map. GIC bases: from the DT, as shown above. SMBIOS strings: what Windows shows in System Information. The 2.50 GHz is the prime core’s max frequency (cpuinfo_max_freq of cpu7 was 2496000 kHz). PlatformSecLib: the SMMU detach The SoC’s PlatformSecLib runs very early. On Qualcomm phones, the display engine (MDP) is behind an SMMU (an IOMMU: it translates device memory accesses the way the MMU translates CPU accesses). The bootloader leaves the display’s SMMU context configured for Android. If we leave it, the display controller’s reads of our framebuffer go through translation tables that do not describe our memory, and the screen stays black or shows garbage. So the SEC library detaches the display’s stream IDs from the SMMU: VOID PlatformInitialize () { // Set MDP SIDs CONST UINT16 MdpStreams[] = { 0x1C00, 0x1C01, 0x1C02 }; // Detach IOMMU Domains ArmSmmuDetach (MdpStreams, ARRAY_SIZE (MdpStreams)); } Palawan’s version had { 0x1C00, 0x1C01, 0x1C04, 0x1C06 }. I took mine from the phone’s DT: the iommus properties of the display nodes (qcom,mdss_mdp@ae00000, qcom,smmu_sde_unsec_cb, qcom,smmu_sde_sec_cb). An iommus property is <phandle streamID mask>, so you read the middle value. adb shell 'cd /sys/firmware/devicetree/base/soc; for n in qcom,mdss_mdp@ae00000 qcom,smmu_sde_unsec_cb qcom,smmu_sde_sec_cb; do echo "$n: $(xxd -p $n/iommus | tr -d "\n")"; done' Also give the copied PlatformSecLib.inf a new FILE_GUID, so it does not clash with Palawan’s copy: python3 -c "import uuid; print(str(uuid.uuid4()).upper())" New GUIDs are right for modules you created (libraries, the platform). They are wrong for anything other code looks up by GUID. Remember this; I did not, a bit further down. Creating the device package: asteroidsPkg Copy the donor and rename everything: cd Platforms mkdir -p Nothing cp -r Realme/bale_bPkg Nothing/asteroidsPkg cd Nothing/asteroidsPkg mv bale_b.dsc asteroids.dsc mv bale_b.dec asteroids.dec mv bale_b.fdf asteroids.fdf grep -rl "bale_b" . | xargs sed -i 's/bale_b/asteroids/g' sed -i 's/PalawanPkg/MilosPkg/g' asteroids.dsc sed -i 's#"Platforms/Realme"#"Platforms/Nothing"#; s#"Silicium-ACPI/Platforms/Realme"#"Silicium-ACPI/Platforms/Nothing"#' DeviceBuild.py Then grep for anything left over from the donor: grep -rn -i "palawan\|realme\|oplus" . What is in the package and what I changed: asteroidsPkg/ asteroids.dsc platform build description asteroids.dec empty, but required asteroids.fdf firmware image layout DeviceBuild.py build settings for stuart (package paths, scopes) Include/APRIORI.inc drivers that must load first, in order Include/DXE.inc all other drivers Include/RAW.inc raw config files (uefiplat.cfg etc) Library/MemoryMapLib/ Library/ConfigurationMapLib/ asteroids.dsc The interesting part: [Defines] PLATFORM_NAME = asteroids PLATFORM_GUID = FFA36E09-833E-4CDD-8955-24E882F40F7F ...
