FLASH_DEFINITION = asteroidsPkg/asteroids.fdf USE_CUSTOM_DISPLAY_DRIVER = 0 !include MilosPkg/MilosPkg.dsc.inc [PcdsFixedAtBuild] gArmTokenSpaceGuid.PcdSystemMemoryBase|0x80000000 gArmPlatformTokenSpaceGuid.PcdCPUCoresStackBase|0xA760D000 gArmPlatformTokenSpaceGuid.PcdCPUCorePrimaryStackSize|0x40000 gSiliciumPkgTokenSpaceGuid.PcdSmbiosSystemManufacturer|"Nothing" gSiliciumPkgTokenSpaceGuid.PcdSmbiosSystemModel|"Phone (3a)" gSiliciumPkgTokenSpaceGuid.PcdSmbiosSystemRetailModel|"asteroids" gSiliciumPkgTokenSpaceGuid.PcdSmbiosSystemRetailSku|"A059" gSiliciumPkgTokenSpaceGuid.PcdSmbiosSystemBoardModel|"Asteroids" gSiliciumPkgTokenSpaceGuid.PcdFrameBufferWidth|1080 gSiliciumPkgTokenSpaceGuid.PcdFrameBufferHeight|2392 gSiliciumPkgTokenSpaceGuid.PcdFrameBufferColorDepth|32 gQcomPkgTokenSpaceGuid.PcdPlatformType|"LA" [LibraryClasses] MemoryMapLib|asteroidsPkg/Library/MemoryMapLib/MemoryMapLib.inf ConfigurationMapLib|asteroidsPkg/Library/ConfigurationMapLib/ConfigurationMapLib.inf [Components] asteroids/AcpiTables.inf PLATFORM_GUID: a new random GUID. This one should be unique per device. PcdSystemMemoryBase: DRAM starts at 0x80000000 on this SoC. Stack base 0xA760D000, size 0x40000: must match the UEFI_Stack region in your memory map. Framebuffer: the display resolution. The framebuffer address comes from the Display_Reserved entry in the memory map (0xE3940000), which is where ABL already left the splash screen. Our firmware draws into the same buffer the bootloader set up. No display driver needed. PcdPlatformType|"LA": Qualcomm drivers come in “LA” (Linux Android) and “WP” (Windows) flavors. Phones have LA drivers. bale_b’s dsc also had a SOC_TYPE define (Palawan has two chip variants); Milos has one, so I removed it. The driver lists Include/APRIORI.inc and Include/DXE.inc list every driver to put in the image. Each Qualcomm driver is referenced by an INF in the Binaries submodule: INF Binaries/asteroids/QcomPkg/Drivers/ClockDxe/ClockDxe.inf INF Binaries/asteroids/QcomPkg/Drivers/PmicDxe/PmicDxeLa.inf INF Binaries/asteroids/QcomPkg/Drivers/UFSDxe/UFSDxe.inf ... The APRIORI order is copied from the donor, and you should not change it unless you know why. Qualcomm’s drivers do not declare all of their real dependencies; they rely on load order. After the copy I removed the lines for drivers my phone does not have (OcdtDxe/OplusProject.inf is an OPPO/Realme-specific driver), and a display panel block in RAW.inc that only applied when USE_CUSTOM_DISPLAY_DRIVER was 1. The Binaries submodule Binaries/<device>/ holds Qualcomm’s driver files for that device, each with a small INF that tells the build what it is. For example, bale_b’s ClockDxe: [Defines] INF_VERSION = 0x0001001B BASE_NAME = ClockDxe FILE_GUID = 4DB5DEA6-5302-4D1A-8A82-677A683B0D29 MODULE_TYPE = DXE_DRIVER VERSION_STRING = 1.0 ENTRY_POINT = EfiEntry [Binaries.AARCH64] DXE_DEPEX|ClockDxe.depex|* PE32|ClockDxe.efi|* [Depex] TRUE The FILE_GUID here is Qualcomm’s GUID for ClockDxe, the same on every phone. That gave me an easy way to generate my whole tree: for every INF in Binaries/bale_b, find the folder file-<same GUID> in my extracted uefi_b, copy its .pe and .depex with the names the INF expects, and write the INF next to them. # genbins.py <reference tree> <extracted uefi> <output tree> import os, re, sys, glob, shutil ref, ext, out = sys.argv[1:4] # index extracted modules by GUID mods = {} for d in glob.glob(f'{ext}/**/file-*', recursive=True): g = os.path.basename(d)[5:].upper() if any(f.endswith(('.pe', '.te', '.raw', '.depex')) for f in os.listdir(d)): mods.setdefault(g, d) missing, done = [], [] for inf in glob.glob(f'{ref}/**/*.inf', recursive=True): rel = os.path.relpath(inf, ref) txt = open(inf).read() guid = re.search(r'FILE_GUID\s*=\s*(\S+)', txt).group(1).upper() if guid not in mods: missing.append(rel); continue src = mods[guid] dst = os.path.join(out, os.path.dirname(rel)); os.makedirs(dst, exist_ok=True) def first(sfx): c = sorted(f for f in os.listdir(src) if f.endswith(sfx)) return os.path.join(src, c[0]) if c else None new = txt for kind, fname in re.findall(r'^\s*(\w+)\|([^|\s]+)\|', txt, re.M): base = fname.replace('.patched', '') # donor's patched files -> stock name s = {'PE32': first('.pe'), 'DXE_DEPEX': first('.depex'), 'TE': first('.te'), 'BIN': first('.raw')}.get(kind) if s is None: print('WARN no section', kind, rel); continue shutil.copyfile(s, os.path.join(dst, base)) new = new.replace(f'|{fname}|', f'|{base}|') open(os.path.join(out, rel), 'w').write(new) done.append(rel) print('generated', len(done)) print('missing:', *missing, sep='\n ') cd Mu-Silicium/Binaries python3 genbins.py bale_b ~/woa/uefi_b asteroids It matched 94 modules. The missing ones were OPPO-specific drivers that only exist on bale_b. Note the .patched handling: the donor’s INFs point at patched binaries (PmicDxeLa.patched.efi). Those are bale_b’s patched files and must never end up in my tree, so the script writes my stock driver under the plain name. Every patch then gets re-found in my own binaries and applied deliberately. Part 3 shows how; I ported bale_b’s eight patches that way before the first boot. Then copy the raw config files (uefiplat.cfg, SecParti.cfg, uefipil.cfg, charger config, panel files) into Binaries/asteroids/RawFiles: mkdir -p asteroids/RawFiles for u in $(find ~/woa/uefi_b -name "*.ui"); do n=$(tr -d '\0' < $u) case "$n" in *.cfg|*.xml|*.bmp|*.csv) r=$(ls $(dirname $u)/*.raw 2>/dev/null | head -1) [ -n "$r" ] && cp $r asteroids/RawFiles/$n;; esac done Finally, check that every INF the include files reference exists: cd Platforms/Nothing/asteroidsPkg for f in $(grep -ho "Binaries/asteroids/[^ ]*\.inf" Include/*.inc | sort -u); do [ -f ../../../$f ] || echo "MISSING $f" done Write a README.md in Binaries/asteroids with the firmware version you extracted from. Future you will want it. I briefly added a RscRtDxe driver that the phone had and bale_b did not. It turned out to be the same module as Mu’s own ReportStatusCodeRouterRuntimeDxe (same GUID), and including both broke the build with a duplicate GUID. If a “new” driver has the same GUID as something Mu already builds from source, leave the binary out. ACPI tables Mu-Silicium gets ACPI tables from the Silicium-ACPI submodule. Each device has an AcpiTables.inf that lists prebuilt .aml files. For a first boot, reusing the closest SoC’s minimal tables is fine: mkdir -p Silicium-ACPI/Platforms/Nothing/asteroids cp Silicium-ACPI/Platforms/Realme/bale_b/AcpiTables.inf Silicium-ACPI/Platforms/Nothing/asteroids/ [Defines] INF_VERSION = 0x00010005 BASE_NAME = AcpiTables FILE_GUID = 7E374E25-8E01-4FEE-87F2-390C23C606CD MODULE_TYPE = USER_DEFINED VERSION_STRING = 1.0 [Binaries] ASL|Common/SSDT.aml ASL|Palawan/APIC.aml ASL|Palawan/DSDT_Minimal.aml ASL|Palawan/FACP.aml ASL|Palawan/GTDT.aml Here is the mistake that cost me most of a day. When I created this file, I had just given the PlatformSecLib copy a new GUID, and I did the same here: I replaced 7E374E25-... with a random one, thinking each device’s INF should be unique. It must not be changed. 7E374E25-8E01-4FEE-87F2-390C23C606CD is the value of PcdAcpiTableStorageFile, defined in MdeModulePkg.dec. The ACPI platform driver searches the firmware for a file with that GUID and installs whatever tables it contains. With a random GUID, the build succeeds, UEFI boots fine, and the driver silently finds nothing. Android does not care. Windows does, and in Part 4 it crashed in a way that took a long breakpoint hunt to trace back here. Quick sanity check you can run on any port: grep -rh FILE_GUID Silicium-ACPI/Platforms/*/*/AcpiTables.inf | sort | uniq -c Every device has the same GUID. If yours is the odd one out, fix it. The build config: asteroids.toml Resources/Configs/<device>.toml tells build_uefi.py how to package the firmware. Copy the donor’s and adjust: # # Boot Shim Configs # [boot_shim] requires_kernel_header = true # # UEFI FD Configs # [uefi_fd] base = 0xA7100000 size = 0x300000 # # Android Boot Image Kernel Configs # [boot_image_kernel] kernel_compression = "gzip" append_dtb = true # # Android Boot Image Configs # [boot_image] header_version = 4 os_version = "17.0.0" os_patch_level = "2026-10" [uefi_fd]: where the firmware image lives in RAM and how big it is. Must match the UEFI_FD entry in the memory map. [boot_shim] and [boot_image_kernel]: make the image look like a gzip-compressed ARM64 Linux kernel with the DTB appended. header_version = 4: the Android boot image header version ABL expects on this phone. You can check the stock boot_b.img header (the version is the 4-byte integer at offset 40 of the header) or just copy what similar phones use. os_version / os_patch_level: see the next section. First boot attempt python3 build_uefi.py -d asteroids -r DEBUG adb reboot bootloader fastboot boot Mu-asteroids.img “Invalid Parameter” ABL refused immediately: Failed to load/authenticate boot image: Invalid Parameter bale_b’s toml did not set os_version and os_patch_level, and its ABL did not mind. Mine did. Newer ABLs check the boot image header’s OS version and patch level against the device’s rollback protection, and an empty value is rejected as invalid. Setting them to the current Android version and a recent month (the two lines at the end of the toml above) fixed it. If ABL rejects the image, compare your boot image header with the stock boot_b.img field by field. unpack_bootimg.py from AOSP (or Mu-Silicium’s own scripts under Resources/Scripts) prints them. The slot problem After one failed attempt, holding power did not bring Android back. The phone went straight to fastboot every time. ABL had counted the failed boot against slot b and marked it unbootable. This fixes it: fastboot set_active b fastboot reboot Do not let the phone fall back to the other slot on its own. On my phone, slot a has different vendor_boot and init_boot, and booting into a mismatched slot can cause more trouble than it solves. It starts With the header fixed, the screen filled with the DEBUG log, scrolling as DXE loaded drivers one by one: Loading driver at 0x000A8xxx000 EntryPoint=0x000A8xxx... DxeCore.efi ... Loading driver at 0x000... ClockDxe.efi ... Loading driver at 0x000... PmicDxe.efi and there it stopped. No crash dump, no error, just the last line sitting there. That is a good result for a first boot: SEC ran, the memory map is good enough for DXE to run, the display works (we can read the log), and twenty-odd Qualcomm drivers loaded and initialized hardware. Something in PmicDxe waits forever, even with bale_b’s PmicDxe patch ported. Committing I committed in small pieces, so the history reads like the bring-up: Milos: Initial support (Silicon/Qualcomm/MilosPkg) asteroids: Initial support (Platforms/Nothing/asteroidsPkg) asteroids: Add DTB (Resources/DTBs/asteroids.dtb) asteroids: Add build config (Resources/Configs/asteroids.toml) Silicium-ACPI: Add asteroids (submodule pointer) Binaries: Add asteroids (submodule pointer) Binaries and Silicium-ACPI are submodules, so commit inside them first (on a branch, since submodules check out in a detached state), then commit the updated pointer in the main repo. Checklist If you are following along with your own phone, by now you should have: A successful build of an existing device A backup of all firmware partitions and the GPT The SoC’s Qualcomm codename and boot branch An SoC package (copied from the closest SoC) with GIC, CPU and SMMU values from your DT A device package (copied from a device on the same boot branch) A memory map converted from xbl_config’s qcom,uefimem node A configuration map from uefiplat.cfg Binaries generated by GUID from your own uefi partition, all stock AcpiTables.inf with FILE_GUID = 7E374E25-8E01-4FEE-87F2-390C23C606CD A toml with the right FD address and boot image header An image that ABL starts, and a log on screen In Part 3 we get past PmicDxe, fix UFS, and work through the rest of the drivers until everything in the status table is green.

title: Windows on the Nothing Phone (3a) - Part 1: The Theory
tags: UEFI, Windows, Qualcomm, Mu-Silicium, ARM64, ACPI
content: Why this series exists I spent a full day getting Mu-Silicium (a UEFI firmware for Snapdragon phones) running on my Nothing Phone (3a), and then getting Windows to boot on top of it. When I started, I went looking for a guide that explained the whole thing end to end. I did not find one. What exists is scattered: a porting page here, a Telegram message there, a repo with patches and no explanation of why they exist. So this is the guide I wanted. It is split into four parts: The theory (this post). Everything you need to understand before touching a single file. Boot chains, ARM64, UEFI, ACPI, how Windows boots, and enough assembly to read a crash dump. Setting up the UEFI project. Tooling, backing up the phone, extracting what we need from the stock firmware, and creating the SoC and device packages. Going green. Fixing every driver until display, storage, buttons, USB and mass storage work in UEFI. Booting Windows. Partitioning, WinPE, a long hunt for a hang, and a full install. The goal is that someone who has never opened a UEFI source tree or looked at Windows internals can read all four and do it themselves. That means this part is long. You can skip sections you already know, but do not skip it entirely. Every problem I hit later was obvious in hindsight once I understood one of the concepts below. The device     Phone Nothing Phone (3a), codename asteroids, model A059 SoC Qualcomm SM7635, Snapdragon 7s Gen 3 Qualcomm’s internal name Milos RAM 8 GB CPU 8 cores in 3 clusters (4 + 3 + 1) Display 1080 x 2392 Software Android 17, bootloader unlocked, adb root works Where things stand at the end of the series: Mu-Silicium boots with display, internal storage, buttons, USB and mass storage working; Windows PE boots to a command prompt and sees the internal storage; and a full Windows 11 install is on the phone. What does “booting” even mean? When you press the power button, the CPU starts executing instructions from a fixed address. It has no idea what an operating system is. Some small piece of code has to set up the hardware enough to load a bigger piece of code, which sets up more hardware and loads an even bigger piece of code, and so on until something big enough (Linux, Windows) is running. That handoff sequence is the boot chain. Every link in the chain has two jobs: Initialize something (DRAM, clocks, storage, display). Find, load, and jump to the next link. The interesting part is what each link tells the next one about the hardware. That turns out to be the whole reason Windows does not “just work” on a phone. How a PC boots On a normal Windows laptop: power on -> UEFI firmware (stored in a SPI flash chip on the motherboard) initializes CPU, RAM, PCIe, USB, storage, display builds ACPI tables that describe the hardware reads the EFI System Partition (ESP) on the disk -> \EFI\Microsoft\Boot\bootmgfw.efi (Windows Boot Manager) -> \Windows\System32\winload.efi (Windows OS Loader) -> ntoskrnl.exe + hal + boot drivers (Windows kernel) Two things matter here: UEFI is a standard interface between firmware and the OS loader. Windows Boot Manager does not care who made your motherboard. It calls standard UEFI functions like “read blocks from this disk” or “give me the memory map”. ACPI is a standard way for firmware to describe hardware to the OS. Windows does not probe for devices on ARM. It reads ACPI tables that say “there is a storage controller at this address, with this interrupt, and its hardware ID is X”. Windows then loads the driver that matches X. Windows requires both. No UEFI, no Boot Manager. No ACPI, no devices. How an Android phone boots A Qualcomm phone boots very differently: power on -> PBL (Primary Boot Loader, burned into the SoC ROM, cannot be changed) -> XBL (eXtensible Boot Loader, initializes DDR, loads the rest) XBL_CONFIG: configuration data, including device trees XBLCore: Qualcomm's own UEFI implementation -> ABL (Android Boot Loader, also called LinuxLoader, a UEFI application) this is where fastboot lives -> Linux kernel from boot.img, with a device tree -> Android Surprise: the phone already runs UEFI. Qualcomm’s XBL contains a full UEFI implementation, built from the same EDK2 code base that PC firmware uses. ABL is literally a UEFI application. So why can’t we just put Windows Boot Manager on the phone and let Qualcomm’s UEFI start it? Qualcomm’s UEFI on phones is configured to boot ABL and nothing else. There is no boot menu, no ESP scanning, no way to choose another loader. It does not provide the ACPI tables Windows needs. Android does not use ACPI; it uses a device tree. It does not leave hardware in a state Windows can use (it turns off USB, puts storage to sleep, and so on, before handing over to Linux). Qualcomm does ship Windows laptops on Snapdragon chips, and on those the same UEFI is built with a different configuration: ACPI, Windows-ready drivers, and so on. Phones just do not get that build. That is the gap Mu-Silicium fills. It is a UEFI firmware we build ourselves, which ABL loads as if it were a Linux kernel, and which then behaves like PC firmware: it scans the ESP, provides ACPI tables, and hands over to Windows Boot Manager. Device tree vs ACPI, the short version Both answer the same question: “what hardware exists, and where?” A device tree (DT) is a data structure. Here is the UFS storage controller on my phone, from the DT that Android boots with: ufshc@1d84000 { compatible = "qcom,ufshc"; reg = <0x1d84000 0x3000>, <0x1d88000 0x18000>; reg-names = "ufs_mem", "ice"; interrupts = <0 0x109 4>; dma-coherent; }; The Linux driver that says compatible = "qcom,ufshc" gets matched to this node, reads reg to find the registers, and interrupts to find its interrupt. ACPI describes the same controller, but in a small bytecode language (AML) that Windows executes: Device (UFS0) { Name (_HID, "QCOM24A5") Name (_UID, 0) Name (_CCA, 1) Name (_CRS, ResourceTemplate () { Memory32Fixed (ReadWrite, 0x01D84000, 0x00015000) Interrupt (ResourceConsumer, Level, ActiveHigh, Exclusive, ,, ) { 0x129 } }) } The Windows driver whose INF file lists ACPI\QCOM24A5 gets loaded for this device. Same information, different language. You will see this exact pair again in Part 4, because writing that ACPI device is what made Windows see the phone’s storage. The interrupt numbers are not the same, and that is not a typo. I explain why in the ACPI section below. ARM64 for people who have never written assembly You will be reading disassembly and crash dumps. You do not need to write assembly fluently. You need to recognize maybe fifteen instructions and understand what the CPU does when something goes wrong. Exception levels: who runs where ARM64 (AArch64) CPUs have four privilege levels, called exception levels: Level Who runs here on a Qualcomm phone EL0 Apps (user space) EL1 OS kernel (Linux, Windows). Our UEFI runs here too. EL2 Hypervisor. On recent Snapdragons: Qualcomm Gunyah EL3 Secure monitor (part of TrustZone firmware) Higher number, more privilege. Code at EL1 cannot touch EL2 or EL3 state. It can ask them for things with special instructions: svc asks EL1 (system call from an app) hvc asks EL2 (hypervisor call) smc asks EL3 (secure monitor call, used for things like PSCI CPU power control and TrustZone apps) There is also a parallel “secure world” where Qualcomm’s trusted OS (QTEE) runs. You can mostly ignore it, except to know that some memory belongs to it and you must not touch that memory. Why the hypervisor matters On older Snapdragons, the bootloader handed the kernel EL2. On recent ones, Qualcomm’s Gunyah hypervisor keeps EL2 and runs Android (and us) at EL1, inside what is effectively a virtual machine. Gunyah uses stage-2 translation: every physical address our code uses goes through a second set of page tables owned by the hypervisor. If our code touches memory that Gunyah did not give us, the access does not just return garbage. It faults. On my phone that showed up as: Synchronous external abort ... FAR 0x80000000 0x80000000 is the start of DRAM, and on this phone the first chunk of it belongs to Gunyah. Our UEFI handed that memory out to Windows Boot Manager as if it were free, and the first read blew up. Part 4 covers this in detail. The lesson for now: a phone’s RAM is not all yours. Large pieces belong to the hypervisor, TrustZone, the modem, and the DSPs. Your firmware’s memory map must mark them as reserved. Registers AArch64 has 31 general-purpose 64-bit registers, x0 to x30. Each one also has a 32-bit view: w0 is the low 32 bits of x0. x0-x7: function arguments. x0 is also the return value. x29: frame pointer. x30: link register (LR). Holds the return address when you call a function. sp: stack pointer. xzr / wzr: a register that always reads as zero. pc: the program counter (address of the current instruction). You cannot write to it directly. UEFI functions return an EFI_STATUS in x0. Zero means EFI_SUCCESS. That single fact is behind half the binary patches in this series: “make this function return success” is mov w0, #0 followed by ret. The instructions you need to recognize mov w0, #0 // w0 = 0 mov w0, wzr // w0 = 0 (same effect, different encoding) ldr w8, [x0] // w8 = 32-bit value read from memory at address x0 str w8, [x1, #0x10] // write w8 to memory at x1 + 0x10 add x0, x1, #0x20 // x0 = x1 + 0x20 adrp x0, 0x12000 // x0 = address of a 4 KiB page, relative to pc bl 0x19184 // call the function at 0x19184 (sets x30 = return address) b 0x3c80 // jump to 0x3c80 (no return) cbz w0, 0x5640 // if w0 == 0, jump to 0x5640 cbnz w0, 0x5640 // if w0 != 0, jump to 0x5640 b.eq 0x493c // jump if the last comparison was "equal" cmp w0, #3 // compare w0 with 3, sets flags for b.eq / b.ne ret // return to the address in x30 nop // do nothing brk #0 // breakpoint: raise an exception on purpose mrs x0, CNTFRQ_EL0 // read a system register into x0 msr VBAR_EL1, x8 // write x8 into a system register That is genuinely most of what you will see in the driver code we patch. Instructions are just 4-byte numbers Every AArch64 instruction is exactly 4 bytes, stored little-endian (least significant byte first). That makes binary patching simple: find the 4 bytes, replace them with 4 other bytes. The encodings I used over and over: Instruction 32-bit value Bytes in the file mov w0, #0 0x52800000 00 00 80 52 mov w0, wzr 0x2A1F03E0 E0 03 1F 2A ret 0xD65F03C0 C0 03 5F D6 nop 0xD503201F 1F 20 03 D5 brk #0 0xD4200000 00 00 20 D4 You do not need to memorize these. llvm-mc will assemble any instruction for you: echo 'mov w0, #0' | llvm-mc -triple=aarch64 -show-encoding # mov w0, #0 // encoding: [0x00,0x00,0x80,0x52] Branches are relative. A bl stores the distance to the target, divided by 4, in its low 26 bits: bl encoding = 0x94000000 | (((target - pc) >> 2) & 0x3FFFFFF) Example: a bl at offset 0x13128 that calls 0x19184: 0x19184 - 0x13128 = 0x605C 0x605C >> 2 = 0x1817 0x94000000 | 0x1817 = 0x94001817 So in the file you would see 17 18 00 94. If you replace that with E0 03 1F 2A (mov w0, wzr), the call never happens and the code continues as if the function returned 0. That is exactly how one of the hangs in Part 3 got fixed. Exceptions, vectors, and reading a crash dump When something goes wrong (reading an unmapped address, executing an invalid instruction, hitting a brk), the CPU takes an exception. It: saves the current pc in ELR_EL1 (Exception Link Register), records why in ESR_EL1 (Exception Syndrome Register), records the faulting memory address (for memory faults) in FAR_EL1 (Fault Address Register), jumps to an address computed from VBAR_EL1 (Vector Base Address Register). VBAR_EL1 points to a table of exception handlers, the vector table. Whoever owns VBAR_EL1 decides what happens on a crash. In UEFI, the firmware installs a handler that prints a register dump to the screen. Once Windows Boot Manager starts, it installs its own vector table, and from then on firmware crash dumps stop appearing. This fact became extremely important in Part 4. A crash dump in Mu-Silicium looks roughly like this (shortened): Synchronous Exception at 0x00000000CE952AA0 ELR 0x00000000CE952AA0 ESR 0x96000007 FAR 0x0000000000000000 How to read it: ELR is the instruction that faulted. FAR is the address it tried to access. 0 means it dereferenced a NULL pointer. ESR tells you the kind of exception. The top 6 bits (bits 31:26) are the exception class (EC): 0x25 = data abort (bad memory access) taken at the same level 0x21 = instruction abort (tried to execute from a bad address) 0x3C = brk instruction 0x15 = svc, 0x16 = hvc, 0x17 = smc For data aborts, the low 6 bits (the DFSC) say what kind of fault: 0x04-0x07 are translation faults at level 0-3 (the address is not mapped at all), 0x10 is a synchronous external abort (the address is mapped but something outside the CPU, like the hypervisor, refused the access). So ESR 0x96000007: 0x96000007 >> 26 = 0x25, a data abort, and 0x07 is a level 3 translation fault. Combined with FAR 0, that is “something read through a NULL pointer”. That one crash is the end of a detective story in Part 4. Turning ELR into a function name An address like 0xCE952AA0 means nothing on its own. You need to know which image was loaded where. UEFI firmware prints a line every time it loads something: Loading driver at 0x000CE78A000 EntryPoint=0x000CE7C8130 bootmgfw.efi So bootmgfw.efi was loaded at 0xCE78A000. The crash at 0xCE952AA0 is at offset 0xCE952AA0 - 0xCE78A000 = 0x1C8AA0 inside it. That offset is an RVA (relative virtual address), and with the right tools (next section) it turns into a function name. Load addresses change between boots. I wasted time once by reusing an old base address. Always read the “Loading driver at” line from the same boot as the crash. Executable files: PE, RVA, VA and file offsets UEFI drivers, Windows Boot Manager, winload and the Windows kernel are all PE/COFF files, the same format as a Windows .exe. You need to understand three kinds of address, because you will convert between them constantly. A PE file contains headers and a list of sections (.text for code, .data, .rdata, and so on). Each section has: a virtual address (where it goes in memory, relative to the image start) a raw pointer (where it is stored in the file) sizes for both The headers also have an ImageBase, the address the image prefers to be loaded at. Term Meaning VA (virtual address) ImageBase + RVA. What disassemblers show if they assume the preferred load address RVA (relative virtual address) Offset from the start of the loaded image File offset Where the bytes actually are in the .efi / .exe file on disk The conversion from VA to file offset: file_offset = section.raw_pointer + (VA - ImageBase - section.virtual_address) where section is the one whose [virtual_address, virtual_address + size) contains VA - ImageBase. For small UEFI drivers built by Qualcomm, sections often have equal virtual and raw offsets, so RVA equals file offset and you can patch at the address the disassembler prints. For big Microsoft binaries that is not true, and if you patch at the wrong offset you corrupt unrelated code. I wrote a ten-line Python helper for this in Part 4; the formula above is all it does. UEFI also uses a stripped-down variant called TE (Terse Executable). Firmware tools extract them as .te files. Same idea, smaller header. Symbols: getting function names for Microsoft binaries Microsoft publishes debug symbols (PDB files) for Windows binaries on a public symbol server. Every PE file contains a “debug directory” entry with a GUID and age that identifies its exact PDB. You can download it from: https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols/<pdb name>/<GUID><age>/<pdb name> For example, the Boot Manager I used had bootmgfw.pdb/C6B0B2AA4429A57378F7820C96619A772. With the PDB, llvm-pdbutil dump -publics gives you every public function name and its location. That turned a raw offset like 0x1C8AA0 into BlUtlGetAcpiTable+0x200, which immediately told me what was going on. Part 4 shows the exact commands. The Qualcomm boot chain in more detail Partitions Phone storage is UFS (Universal Flash Storage). It is split into several LUNs (logical units), each of which looks like a separate disk to Linux: /dev/block/sda, sdb, … sdf. Each has its own GPT partition table. The big one, sda, holds userdata (your Android data). Firmware partitions live on the others. The ones relevant to us: Partition Contents xbl_a/b XBL, the first loader after the ROM xbl_config_a/b XBL configuration, including embedded device trees with the UEFI memory map uefi_a/b Qualcomm’s UEFI firmware volume: all the DXE drivers we will reuse abl_a/b ABL / fastboot boot_a/b Android boot image (kernel). We never flash this userdata Android data. We shrink it to make room for Windows Android uses symbolic links so you do not have to know which sdX a partition is on: ls -l /dev/block/by-name/ Always use these names. On my phone, the letter of the main LUN changed between boots once (it showed up as sdc), and a script using /dev/block/sda14 would have written to the wrong place. A/B slots Most partitions exist twice, _a and _b. The phone boots from one slot and updates the other, so a bad update can fall back. Check the active slot with: adb shell getprop ro.boot.slot_suffix # _b on my phone fastboot getvar current-slot Extract firmware from the active slot. The inactive slot may have a different firmware version. fastboot boot vs fastboot flash fastboot boot image.img # load into RAM and boot once, nothing written fastboot flash boot image.img # write it to the boot partition, permanent Mu-Silicium is always tested with fastboot boot. It replaces nothing. Hold the power button to reboot and the phone boots Android as normal. This is what makes the whole project safe to experiment with: you can try fifty broken firmware builds in an afternoon and the phone is fine. One time a failed fastboot boot made ABL mark my active slot as unbootable, and the phone kept coming back to fastboot instead of Android. fastboot set_active b (your active slot) clears that flag. What the unlocked bootloader gives us With a locked bootloader, ABL refuses to boot images that are not signed by the vendor. Unlocking lets ABL boot any boot image you hand it with fastboot boot. It does not let you replace XBL or Qualcomm’s UEFI (those are verified by the ROM with keys burned into the chip). That is fine; we do not need to. We run our firmware after ABL, as its “kernel”. UEFI from zero UEFI is a specification. EDK2 (from TianoCore) is the open source reference implementation. Almost every UEFI firmware in existence, including Qualcomm’s, is built from EDK2. Phases UEFI firmware runs in phases: SEC -> PEI -> DXE -> BDS -> (OS loader runs) -> RT Phase What happens SEC (Security) First code. Sets up a stack, finds the next phase PEI (Pre-EFI Initialization) Minimal hardware init. Builds “HOBs” (hand-off blocks) describing memory DXE (Driver Execution Environment) The big phase. Loads dozens of drivers that initialize everything BDS (Boot Device Selection) Decides what to boot. Scans disks, runs the boot loader TSL (Transient System Load) The OS loader (Windows Boot Manager) is running and still using firmware services RT (Runtime) After the OS takes over. Only a few “runtime services” remain (clock, variables, reset) On our phone, Mu-Silicium does SEC and a simplified PEI itself (DRAM is already initialized by XBL, so there is little to do), then runs DXE with a mix of open source drivers and Qualcomm’s closed-source drivers, then BDS boots Windows Boot Manager from the ESP. Drivers, protocols, handles DXE is a bunch of independent drivers. They talk to each other through protocols. A protocol is a struct of function pointers, identified by a GUID (a 128-bit ID like 964E5B21-6459-11D2-8E39-00A0C969723B). A driver installs a protocol on a handle (an opaque object). Another driver locates that protocol by GUID and calls its functions. For example, the UFS driver installs EFI_BLOCK_IO_PROTOCOL on a handle for each LUN. The partition driver finds every Block IO handle, reads the GPT, and installs a new Block IO handle per partition. The FAT driver finds partitions with a FAT filesystem and installs EFI_SIMPLE_FILE_SYSTEM_PROTOCOL. BDS then looks for a file system containing \EFI\Boot\bootaa64.efi. This layering is why a broken driver deep in the stack (say, the PMIC driver hanging forever) prevents everything above it from running. The DEBUG build prints Loading driver at ... XYZ.efi for each driver. The last line on the screen when it hangs tells you which driver is stuck. Driver load order and APRIORI DXE drivers declare dependencies ([Depex]): “I need protocols X and Y before I can start.” The DXE dispatcher runs drivers whose dependencies are satisfied. Some drivers must run first no matter what; those are listed in an APRIORI list in the firmware image. Qualcomm’s drivers rely heavily on a fixed APRIORI order. Boot Services, Runtime Services, ExitBootServices The firmware provides two tables of functions: Boot Services: memory allocation (AllocatePages, GetMemoryMap), loading images (LoadImage, StartImage), protocols, events, timers. Runtime Services: get/set time, UEFI variables, reset the system. When the OS loader is ready to take over the machine, it calls ExitBootServices(). After that: Boot Services are gone. Calling one is a bug. The firmware’s drivers get a final callback to shut their hardware down cleanly. The OS owns all memory except what is marked Runtime or Reserved. That “shut down cleanly” step matters a lot on phones. Qualcomm’s USB driver, for example, turns the USB controller off at ExitBootServices because Linux will re-initialize it. Windows expects the firmware to leave some hardware usable. Several binary patches in Part 3 exist only to stop drivers from turning things off. The memory map The firmware keeps a map of all memory: every range, its type, and its attributes. Windows Boot Manager reads it with GetMemoryMap() and decides where to put itself, the kernel, and everything else. Memory types you will see: Type Meaning EfiConventionalMemory Free RAM, anyone can use it EfiLoaderCode / EfiLoaderData Used by the OS loader EfiBootServicesCode/Data Used by firmware, becomes free after ExitBootServices EfiRuntimeServicesCode/Data Used by firmware forever, the OS must not touch it EfiReservedMemoryType Do not touch, ever EfiMemoryMappedIO Device registers, not RAM On a PC, the firmware discovers the memory map. On our phone, we write it by hand in a C file, because the phone has many ranges of RAM owned by other things (hypervisor, modem, TrustZone) and the firmware has no way to know that by itself. Getting this table wrong was the first Windows crash in Part 4. Firmware volumes, FD, FFS The firmware is built into a Flash Device image (FD): one binary blob, loaded at a fixed address. Inside are Firmware Volumes (FV), which are like tiny filesystems. Each file in a volume is an FFS file identified by a GUID, and contains sections: Section Contents PE32 / TE Executable code UI Human-readable name (PmicDxe) DXE_DEPEX Dependency expression RAW Arbitrary data (config files, ACPI tables, logos) Qualcomm’s uefi_b partition is exactly this: a firmware volume full of DXE drivers. A tool called uefi-firmware-parser can unpack it into a directory tree, one folder per file GUID, with the UI name in a separate file. That is how we get Qualcomm’s drivers in Part 2. File GUIDs are how firmware code finds data. The ACPI tables, for example, are stored as a RAW file with a specific GUID, and the ACPI driver looks for exactly that GUID. If you give the file a different GUID, nothing complains at build time. The driver just never finds your tables. I did exactly this, and it cost me most of a day. Remember it. The ESP and the default boot path The EFI System Partition is a FAT32 partition with a GPT type code of EF00. UEFI firmware can read FAT32 natively. When there is no boot entry configured, firmware tries the removable media fallback path: \EFI\Boot\bootaa64.efi (ARM64) \EFI\Boot\bootx64.efi (x86-64) Windows also installs itself at \EFI\Microsoft\Boot\bootmgfw.efi, and puts a copy at the fallback path. Mu-Silicium’s BDS scans for these, so putting Windows Boot Manager on the ESP is enough to boot it. EDK2 and Project Mu: how the source is organized EDK2 has its own build system with its own file types. You will edit all of these: File Purpose .dec (declaration) Declares a package: its GUIDs, PCDs, library classes, include paths .dsc (description) Describes a platform build: which modules to build, which library implementation to use for each library class, PCD values .fdf (flash description) Describes the firmware image: which modules go into which firmware volume, in what order, APRIORI lists .inf (information) Describes one module (driver, library, application, or a prebuilt binary): sources, dependencies, FILE_GUID A few more concepts: Package: a directory with a .dec, like MdeModulePkg or ArmPkg. Platforms in Mu-Silicium are packages too (asteroidsPkg). Library class: an interface (like MemoryMapLib). The .dsc picks which implementation (which .inf) to link. This is how a device provides its own memory map without changing shared code: it implements MemoryMapLib and the .dsc points to it. PCD (Platform Configuration Database): named configuration values. gArmTokenSpaceGuid.PcdGicDistributorBase|0x17100000 sets the GIC base for the build. Some are fixed at build time, some can change at runtime. FILE_GUID: each module’s identity inside the firmware image. For prebuilt binaries it must match what other code expects. Project Mu is Microsoft’s fork of EDK2, the one Surface devices use. It adds a Python-based build wrapper (“stuart”), split repositories, and a lot of quality-of-life features. Mu-Silicium is built on Project Mu. Mu-Silicium: how it works on a phone Mu-Silicium is a Project Mu platform for Snapdragon phones. The trick that makes it work: We build a UEFI FD image. The build script wraps it in an Android boot image, the same format as a Linux kernel boot.img, with a small “boot shim” in front so it looks like an ARM64 Linux kernel. The phone’s device tree is appended, the same way a real kernel image carries one. ABL loads it like any kernel, and jumps to it. Our UEFI starts from SEC, sets up its own memory map, and runs DXE from scratch: its own core, plus Qualcomm’s driver binaries extracted from the phone. BDS boots Windows Boot Manager from the ESP. Why reuse Qualcomm’s drivers? Because the hardware documentation for clocks, power management (PMIC), UFS, display and USB on these SoCs is not public. Writing those drivers from scratch would be a multi-year project per SoC. Qualcomm’s binaries already know how to drive the hardware. They just have assumptions baked in (about which bootloader started them, what state the hardware is in, what runs after them) that we fix with small binary patches. Repository layout Mu-Silicium/ build_uefi.py the build entry point Status.md what works on each device Platforms/<Vendor>/<device>Pkg/ one package per phone <device>.dsc / .fdf / .dec DeviceBuild.py Include/APRIORI.inc, DXE.inc, RAW.inc driver lists for the FDF Library/MemoryMapLib/ the hand-written memory map Library/ConfigurationMapLib/ Qualcomm config values Silicon/Qualcomm/<SoC>Pkg/ one package per SoC (shared by phones) Silicon/Qualcomm/QcomPkg/ shared Qualcomm code Silicon/Silicium/SiliciumPkg/ shared Silicium code (KEP, logo, etc) Binaries/ submodule: extracted Qualcomm drivers per device Silicium-ACPI/ submodule: ACPI tables per SoC and device Mu_Basecore/ submodule: Project Mu core (EDK2 fork) Resources/Configs/<device>.toml build settings (FD address, boot image header) Resources/DTBs/<device>.dtb device tree appended to the boot image The split between Silicon/Qualcomm/<SoC>Pkg and Platforms/<Vendor>/<device>Pkg matters. Everything that is the same for every phone with that chip (GIC addresses, CPU count, SMMU setup) goes in the SoC package. Everything specific to one phone (memory map, display size, which driver binaries) goes in the device package. Status.md has a table per device: Display, Internal Storage, Side Buttons, USB Host Mode, USB Device Mode, USB Power Delivery, Mass Storage, Windows Boot, Linux Boot. Part 3 is about turning that table green. Mass storage mode One feature worth understanding now: Mu-Silicium can expose the phone’s internal storage to a PC over USB, as a USB Mass Storage device (like a USB stick). On other devices this is how people install Windows: boot UEFI, plug into a PC, and the PC sees the phone’s whole disk. I ended up not being able to use it on my work laptop (Part 3 explains why), and did the install a different way. KEP: the Kernel Errata Patcher Windows has expectations about ARM CPUs that some Qualcomm chips do not meet: certain system registers being implemented, a specific GIC behavior, a PSCI call working. Windows on real Snapdragon laptops has workarounds that are switched on for specific chips; phones do not match those. Mu-Silicium’s Kernel Errata Patcher (KEP) hooks into the boot process, follows Windows Boot Manager, then winload, and patches the Windows kernel in memory right before it starts to avoid those instructions. The SoC package declares which errata apply: HAS_ACTLR_EL1_UNIMPLEMENTED_ERRATA = 1 HAS_AMCNTENSET0_EL0_UNIMPLEMENTED_ERRATA = 1 HAS_GIC_V3_WITHOUT_IRM_FLAG_SUPPORT_ERRATA = 1 HAS_PSCI_MEMPROTECT_FAILING_ERRATA = 0 You do not need to understand the details yet. Just know that KEP exists, that it reads memory the boot loader allocated, and that it was the first thing to crash when my memory map was wrong. ACPI from zero The table chain ACPI is a set of binary tables in memory. Windows finds them like this: UEFI configuration table (GUID for ACPI 2.0) -> RSDP (Root System Description Pointer) -> XSDT (eXtended System Description Table): a list of 64-bit pointers -> FACP (FADT) fixed hardware info, points to the DSDT -> APIC (MADT) interrupt controller and CPU list -> GTDT generic timers -> DSDT the main device description, in AML -> SSDT extra device descriptions, in AML -> PPTT, DBG2, BGRT, CSRT ... Every table starts with the same 36-byte header: a 4-character signature (APIC, DSDT…), length, revision, checksum, OEM ID, OEM table ID. The tables that matter for a minimal Windows boot on ARM: Table What Windows gets from it FACP (FADT) Basic platform flags, PSCI support, pointer to the DSDT APIC (MADT) The GIC distributor and redistributor addresses, and one entry per CPU (with its MPIDR) GTDT Which interrupts the architected timers use DSDT Every other device SSDT More devices (Mu-Silicium uses a common SSDT for its own bits) Others you will meet: BGRT (boot logo, so Windows can keep showing it), PPTT (CPU topology and caches), DBG2 (debug port), CSRT (core system resources, used by Qualcomm’s Windows drivers for things like DMA controllers). ASL and AML Device descriptions in the DSDT are not plain data. They are written in ASL (ACPI Source Language), compiled into AML (ACPI Machine Language) bytecode, and the OS has an interpreter that runs it. That lets methods compute things at runtime (for example, return a different status depending on a variable). The compiler is iasl, from Intel’s ACPICA project. It also decompiles: iasl -d table.aml produces readable ASL. Objects you will see in every device Device (UFS0) // a device named UFS0 { Name (_HID, "QCOM24A5") // Hardware ID: the driver matches this Name (_CID, "...") // Compatible ID: fallback match Name (_UID, 0) // Unique ID, to tell two identical devices apart Name (_CCA, 1) // Cache Coherency Attribute: 1 = DMA is cache-coherent Name (_CRS, ResourceTemplate () { // Current Resource Settings Memory32Fixed (...) // register range Interrupt (...) // interrupt }) Method (_STA) { Return (0x0F) } // Status: 0x0F = present, enabled, shown, working Device (DEV0) { // a child device Name (_ADR, 8) // address on the parent bus Name (_RMV, 0) // not removable } } A Windows driver package has an INF file that lists hardware IDs it supports: [Qualcomm.NTarm64] %ACPI\QCOM24A5.DeviceDesc%=UfsQualcomm8996Install, ACPI\QCOM24A5 When Windows sees a device with _HID QCOM24A5, it builds the ID ACPI\QCOM24A5, finds that line, and loads the driver. That line is from Windows’ own built-in UFS driver (storufs.inf). It is why Windows could see my phone’s storage without any extra driver package, once the ACPI had a device with that _HID. Interrupt numbers: DT vs ACPI ARM’s GIC interrupt controller numbers interrupts like this: Range Type 0-15 SGI (software-generated, used between CPUs) 16-31 PPI (private per CPU, like the timer) 32+ SPI (shared peripherals) A device tree writes interrupts as <type number flags>, where type 0 means SPI and the number is counted from the start of the SPI range. ACPI uses the absolute number, called the GSIV (Global System Interrupt Vector). So: DT: interrupts = <0 0x109 4> -> SPI 0x109 ACPI: GSIV = 0x109 + 32 = 0x129 That is why the UFS interrupt is 0x109 in the device tree and 0x129 in the ACPI table above. Getting this wrong gives you a device that initializes and then times out on every command, because its interrupts go nowhere. How Windows boots, step by step The pieces File Where Job bootmgfw.efi ESP \EFI\Microsoft\Boot\ Windows Boot Manager. Reads the BCD, picks an entry, loads the OS loader BCD ESP \EFI\Microsoft\Boot\BCD Boot Configuration Data: the boot menu and settings, stored as a registry hive winload.efi \Windows\System32\ OS Loader. Loads the kernel, HAL, registry SYSTEM hive and boot drivers, calls ExitBootServices ntoskrnl.exe \Windows\System32\ The kernel boot drivers \Windows\System32\drivers\ Drivers needed to reach the boot disk (storage, file system) The flow: Mu-Silicium BDS -> bootmgfw.efi initializes its own library (memory manager, ACPI access, TPM, crypto) opens the BCD, picks the default entry loads winload.efi (from disk, or from a RAM disk for WinPE) -> winload.efi loads ntoskrnl, hal, SYSTEM hive, boot-start drivers builds the kernel's memory map and page tables calls ExitBootServices jumps to the kernel -> ntoskrnl phase 0: CPU, memory manager, HAL, interrupt controller, timers (from ACPI) phase 1: start the other CPUs, load drivers, mount the boot disk -> smss.exe -> ... -> login screen or Windows Setup The kernel needs the boot disk by name (the BCD stores which partition Windows is on). If no driver can see the disk, you get the classic INACCESSIBLE_BOOT_DEVICE blue screen. That is why the UFS ACPI device matters so much: without it, a full Windows install cannot boot even if everything else is perfect. The BCD The BCD is a registry hive with “objects” (boot entries, identified by GUIDs) and “elements” (settings, identified by hex IDs). On Windows you edit it with bcdedit. A few settings we will use: bcdedit /set {default} testsigning on # allow test-signed drivers bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled no # do not jump into recovery on failure bcdedit /set {default} bootstatuspolicy IgnoreAllFailures bcdedit /set {default} nointegritychecks on bcdedit /set {bootmgr} bootdebug off On Linux you can read and modify it with tools that understand registry hives (I used the Python library regipy to read it). WinPE Windows PE (Preinstallation Environment) is a small Windows that runs entirely from RAM. It is what the Windows installer and recovery environment run on. It ships as a .wim file (boot.wim) that Boot Manager loads into a RAM disk, using boot.sdi as the RAM disk template. For a port it is perfect as a first target: It needs no disk drivers to boot, because it lives in RAM. It gives you a command prompt with diskpart, dism, bcdboot, bcdedit. If it boots, the CPU, memory, interrupt controller, timers and ACPI basics all work. WIM and ESD files Windows images are distributed as WIM (Windows Imaging Format) or ESD (a more heavily compressed WIM). One file can hold several images (indexes), for example Home and Pro editions. On Linux, wimlib (wimlib-imagex) can list, extract, modify and apply them, including applying straight onto an NTFS filesystem while keeping Windows permissions and special file types intact. That is how I installed Windows without a Windows PC. Inside every install image there is a recovery environment at \Windows\System32\Recovery\winre.wim. WinRE is a WinPE with extra recovery tools. With one small change (deleting the file that launches the recovery UI) it drops you to a plain command prompt. That is the WinPE I used. Debugging without a debugger On a PC you would attach a serial cable or a kernel debugger. On this phone I had neither: no exposed UART, and Windows’ network debugging needs a supported USB or network adapter. The tools that actually worked: Read the screen. The DEBUG build of Mu-Silicium prints its log to the display. The last line before a hang is your first clue. Bisect with modified binaries. Make a copy of the driver that skips half its work. If the hang moves, the problem is in the half you skipped. Repeat. Write diagnostics to the ESP. Add code to the firmware that writes text files (memory map, ACPI tables, benchmark results) to the ESP. Reboot into Android, mount the ESP, read the files. This is far more reliable than taking phone photos of tiny text. Breakpoints as checkpoints. Replace one instruction in a binary with brk #0. If execution reaches it, you get a crash dump that proves it. If not, the problem is earlier. Move the breakpoint and repeat. It is slow, one reboot per test, but it works on code you have no source for. Part 4 is mostly this technique. The common idea in all of them: binary search. Every test should cut the space where the bug can be in half. Prerequisites Hardware: A Snapdragon phone with an unlockable bootloader, unlocked. Ideally one whose SoC is already supported (or close to one that is) in Mu-Silicium. A USB cable and a Linux PC (I used Ubuntu). Windows works too for some steps, but every command in this series is for Linux. Patience, and a phone you are willing to factory reset. Repartitioning wipes Android data. On the phone: Root access. On my phone the ROM is a userdebug build, so adb root gives a root shell directly. On a retail build you would use Magisk and su. You need root to read firmware partitions and to repartition. Basic tools available as root: sgdisk, and ideally mkfs.ntfs / newfs_msdos. Mine had all of them. Knowledge: Comfortable in a Linux shell. Able to read C. Most of what you edit is tables and config, not algorithms. Python helps a lot. Almost every investigation step was a small Python script. Software (Part 2 installs everything): Tool Used for git, python3, pip Mu-Silicium’s build system clang / LLVM 18 (llvm-objdump, llvm-mc, llvm-pdbutil, llvm-symbolizer) Disassembling, assembling single instructions, reading PDBs, symbolizing crashes uefi_firmware (pip) Unpacking Qualcomm’s UEFI partition fdt (pip) or dtc Reading device trees adb, fastboot Talking to the phone wimtools (wimlib) Working with Windows images ntfs-3g (mkntfs) Creating NTFS images on Linux img2simg (android-sdk-libsparse-utils) Converting raw images to fastboot sparse images iasl Compiling ACPI tables xxd, strings, grep -boa Poking at binaries Before you continue If you remember only a few things from this post: The phone already runs UEFI, but not one Windows can use. Mu-Silicium is our own UEFI, loaded by ABL as if it were a kernel. Our firmware runs at EL1 under a hypervisor. Memory that belongs to someone else must be marked reserved, or things fault. UEFI drivers find each other by GUID. A wrong GUID fails silently. Windows needs ACPI. No tables, no Windows. No storage device in the DSDT, no disk. Crashes come with ELR, ESR and FAR. ELR minus the image base gives an RVA, and a PDB turns an RVA into a function name. When you have no debugger, bisect. In Part 2 we set up the tools, back up the phone, pull apart the stock firmware, and create the SoC and device packages for the first boot attempt.

title: Inside libGoogleFeed, and Writing My Own -1 Screen
tags: Android, AOSP, Launcher3, Reverse Engineering, Frameworks
content: What this is? Part two of the Launcher3 post. That one was the map. This one is the part I actually went down a hole for: what sits to the left of your home screen, what is inside the jar every ROM ships to get it, and what it takes to replace that jar with something you wrote. Whose code runs when you swipe? Swipe past the first home screen and a panel slides in. Quick question: whose code just drew that? Not the launcher’s. This took me longer to accept than it should have. I kept looking for the view. There is no view. Why -1 is not just another page Put the two side by side:   A workspace page The -1 panel What it is a CellLayout in your view tree not a view at all Where it lives rows in the launcher database not in the model Whose process yours another app entirely The launcher never draws the panel. It only forwards your finger, and gets back a number saying how far open the panel is. AOSP ships the socket and no plug Remember those 434 lines in src_plugins/ from the last post? This is what they are for. Launcher3 defines the entire overlay contract, and then implements none of it. The default is literally an empty object: protected LauncherOverlayManager getDefaultOverlay() { return new LauncherOverlayManager() { }; } That is it. That is the whole extension point. Override that one method and the -1 screen is yours. Every OEM feed, every custom launcher’s left panel, goes through this. AOSP ships you the socket and no plug. The protocol The overlay lives in another process, so the two sides talk over binder: The interface — ILauncherOverlay.aidl, 17 methods. Scroll, attach, detach, open, close, activity state. The handshake — the launcher binds an intent with action com.android.launcher3.WINDOW_OVERLAY and data app://<launcher-package>:<launcher-uid>. The provider checks that pair against the calling UID before handing back a binder. The negotiation — a service.api.version meta-data tag on the service. The client gates features on it: version 3 unlocks windowAttached2, 4 unlocks setActivityState, 7 unlocks redraw. Nothing about that is Google-specific. It is a versioned, authenticated, plain AIDL service. Only the implementation on the other end is closed. Inside libGoogleFeed.jar Most ROMs ship Google’s feed by dropping in a prebuilt jar and wiring a config flag. I wanted to know what was actually in it, so I pulled it apart. Decompiled it is about 1,300 lines, and half the class names are single letters: com/google/android/libraries/gsa/launcherclient/LauncherClient.java com/google/android/libraries/gsa/launcherclient/a.java com/google/android/libraries/gsa/launcherclient/b.java com/google/android/libraries/gsa/launcherclient/c.java ... com/google/android/libraries/a/a.java # ILauncherOverlay, obfuscated com/google/android/libraries/a/c.java The obfuscated interface is exactly what you would expect once you line it up: public interface c extends IInterface { void d() throws RemoteException; // startScroll void e(float f) throws RemoteException; // onScroll void f() throws RemoteException; // endScroll void g(WindowManager.LayoutParams p, e cb, int i) // windowAttached ... } And here is the part that made the whole thing click. Compare the jar against the open-source client:   Google’s jar Open-source client Bind action com.android.launcher3.WINDOW_OVERLAY com.android.launcher3.WINDOW_OVERLAY Interface descriptor com.google.android.libraries.launcherclient.ILauncherOverlay same string, exactly Talks to com.google.android.googlequicksearchbox, hardcoded any package you point it at Same door, same handshake. The jar is not magic. It is a client, hardcoded to one provider, and you can write your own. (For the curious: the jar negotiates a newer protocol than the open client does, v10/cv19 against v7/cv9. The handshake itself is identical, which is exactly why a from-source client works at all.) Building my own So I did. The project is split the way you would expect: Launcher3Feed ├── core/ # reusable overlay base ├── google-gsa/ # the server side of ILauncherOverlay └── helloworld/ # a minimal provider, ~5 lines of glue The provider side is four steps: Export a service — answer the overlay action, declare your api version Check the caller — the launcher names its package and UID, verify both Own a window — the launcher passes its LayoutParams, you add your panel beside it Fill it — anything you like The sample provider really is this small: class HelloWorldOverlayService : FeedOverlayService() { override fun createOverlay(context: Context): FeedOverlay = HelloWorldOverlay(context) } class HelloWorldOverlay(context: Context) : FeedOverlay(context) { override fun onCreateContentView(inflater: LayoutInflater, container: ViewGroup): View = inflater.inflate(R.layout.overlay_layout, container, false) } And there it is. No Google app, no prebuilt jar, no network dependency: Not much to look at yet. But that is my window, in my process, on the -1 screen. Two things that cost me a day each AIDL numbers its methods by position My server was written against a different revision of ILauncherOverlay than the launcher was. The interface names matched. The transaction codes did not: code launcher sends my app ran 5 windowDetached() requestVoiceDetection() 6 closeOverlay() nothing, unhandled 10 requestVoiceDetection() windowDetached() 16 setActivityState() closeOverlay() Codes 1 to 4 matched, so scrolling worked perfectly and everything else was subtly wrong. Code 16 was the worst: at api version 7 the launcher calls setActivityState() on every onStart/onResume/onPause/onStop, and my side was running closeOverlay() on it. The panel closed itself every time you came back to the launcher. Lesson: do not count methods by hand. Run the aidl compiler and read the generated codes: prebuilts/build-tools/linux-x86/bin/aidl -I<dir> -o<out> ILauncherOverlay.aidl grep TRANSACTION_ out/.../ILauncherOverlay.java Insert one method in the middle of an AIDL and every call after it silently means something else. The upstream change that does not conflict I mentioned this in the last post. Here is the real version. Moving my overlay patches from Android 16 to 17, git reported four conflicts. All four were easy, mechanical stuff. The change that actually broke the feed produced no conflict at all. Upstream had deleted the onAttachedToWindow and onDetachedFromWindow calls into the overlay. Lines my patch had never touched, so git had nothing to say. The effect: LauncherClient only sets its mLayoutParams inside onAttachedToWindow, and every overlay call is gated behind a null check on it. So the client bound fine, connected fine, logged nothing unusual, and drew nothing. Conflicts are the changes that announce themselves. Audit the call sites your patch depends on, not just the lines it edits. What is next The helloworld panel proves the plumbing. The interesting question is what to actually put in it. What I am chasing now is bridging the Glanceable Hub into the -1 screen, so the panel shows the same widget instances as the lock screen rather than a second copy. SystemUI already built most of the machinery for this in Android 17, for its own reasons, and it streams RemoteViews for widget ids you do not own. That is a whole post of its own. Once it is not held together with tape. If you want to poke at this The short version for anyone who wants to try: Read src_plugins/, all 434 lines Find getDefaultOverlay() in Launcher.java Write a service that answers com.android.launcher3.WINDOW_OVERLAY Generate the AIDL, do not trust the method order The -1 screen is a bound service, not a Google feature. Anyone can replace it. title: Launcher3: Architecture and Internals
tags: Android, AOSP, Launcher3, Frameworks, SystemUI
content: What this is? Notes from a year of carrying Launcher3 patches across Android releases. Not a tutorial on writing a launcher, more like the map I wish someone had handed me before I started rebasing this thing every six months. Ain’t gonna explain “what is a home screen”. Launcher3 is not an app drawer The first thing that surprised me is how much of the Android experience actually lives inside this one app. It is not one screen. It is six surfaces living in one process, and you move between them constantly without noticing: Home / Workspace — pages of icons, folders, the hotseat All Apps — the drawer and its search box Widgets — other apps drawing inside yours Overview — Recents, live system tasks Taskbar — on tablets, always on screen The -1 screen — the odd one out, which gets its own post Recents is the one that trips people up. It is not a system screen. The launcher renders your live tasks. The source split Before reading any code, look at how the tree is divided. This tells you more than any doc: packages/apps/Launcher3 ├── src/ # the launcher proper ├── quickstep/ # the half that needs platform privileges ├── src_plugins/ # interfaces only, the plugin seam └── ... Rough numbers from the Android 17 tree I work in: directory files lines src/ 780 ~146,000 quickstep/src/ 619 ~158,000 src_plugins/ 9 434 That last row is not a typo. Around 300,000 lines of launcher, and the entire plugin surface is 434 lines. Everything that is allowed to plug in from outside Launcher3 goes through those nine files. Keep that number in your head, it becomes important in the next post. The src/ vs quickstep/ split is the practical one. src/ builds without system privileges. quickstep/ links against SystemUI’s shared libraries and will not build unless you are on the platform. If your change does not compile and you cannot work out why, check which half you are in. A mental model Six names get you oriented in any Launcher3 tree, from any Android version. On the view side: Launcher — the Activity. Around 2,900 lines of lifecycle and wiring. Workspace — the pager that holds your home screens DragLayer — sits above everything, owns anything you can drag And the three things that drive them: LauncherModel — what exists (apps, shortcuts, widgets, the database) DeviceProfile — how big everything is, derived per device and posture StateManager — which surface is showing (NORMAL, ALL_APPS, OVERVIEW …) Views on the left, drivers on the right. Most launcher bugs you will chase are a state that disagrees with a profile. I will come back to that. What happens when you unlock This is the part I find genuinely well designed, and it explains why unlock feels instant. Activity starts — inflate the views, work out the grid for this device Loader wakes up — a worker thread opens the launcher database Load in stages — workspace first, then all apps, then shortcuts, then widgets Bind and draw — items come back to the UI thread, first frame The staging is deliberate and it is visible in the code. LoaderTask literally logs its own phases: logASplit("step 1 loading workspace complete"); logASplit("step 2 loading AllApps complete"); logASplit("step 3 loading all shortcuts complete"); Your home screen is drawable before the app drawer has finished loading. You can watch these in a systrace if you want to see where your boot time actually goes. The workspace is a grid of grids The view hierarchy is simpler than it looks once you see the nesting: Workspace the pager CellLayout one page, a fixed grid a cell icon, folder or widget Hotseat a CellLayout that never scrolls Three things follow from this: Every page is the same grid, sized by DeviceProfile A folder is just a cell that opens into another grid Drag and drop lifts a view into the DragLayer, which sits above everything That last one is why the drag target chrome renders over your pages rather than inside them: And All Apps is its own surface, not a workspace page: The launcher is not an island This is the bit that surprises people who have only read src/. Launcher3 and SystemUI are in constant conversation: Recents is not a system screen. The launcher renders your live tasks. Swipe-up-to-home is a SystemUI gesture handed to launcher code mid-animation. That handoff is exactly why the quickstep/ half needs platform privileges to build at all. If you are forking Launcher3 for a ROM, this is the coupling that will bite you on every platform bump. Your launcher does not fail alone, it fails together with whatever SystemUI shipped that release. Things that actually bite A short list of what has cost me the most time: Grids and DeviceProfile. Stay scared of these. Every dimension on screen comes out of a profile, and profiles are derived per device, per posture, per display size. A change that looks right on your phone will look wrong on a tablet, in landscape, or with a non-default display size. Database migration between grid sizes is its own special pain. State transitions. When something looks visually broken, my first check is no longer the view code. It is which LauncherState we are in and which DeviceProfile was active when the layout ran. Upstream changes that do not conflict. This one deserves its own paragraph. Git only warns you about lines you edited. It says nothing about call sites you depend on. I have had a patch rebase perfectly clean, compile, boot, and do nothing at all, because upstream deleted the call site that used to invoke my code. More on this in the next post, where it happened to me for real. Where to start reading If you want to actually go through the source, this order worked for me: Launcher.java — read onCreate end to end, ignore everything else LoaderTask.java — follow the three steps DeviceProfile.java — skim it, then keep it open forever Workspace.java and CellLayout.java — the grid src_plugins/ — all 434 lines, it takes ten minutes Step five is the one nobody does, and it is the one that opens up the -1 screen, which is where I have spent most of my time lately. That is the next post: what actually sits to the left of your home screen, what is inside libGoogleFeed.jar, and how to replace it with something you wrote yourself.
